prompt: Some friends are having a conversation about how boring things have gotten ... in the middle of a comically dramatic / dangerous / or otherwise intense scene .
content:
# Rope Bridge, Third Tuesday

The bridge had gone at the left anchor, which was the one Dov had said looked fine.

"I said it looked *fine*," Dov said, from where he dangled by one gauntlet. "I didn't say it *was* fine. Those are different statements."

"Nobody's blaming you," said Marguerite, who was blaming him. She hung from a plank two feet below, boots swinging over a river of lava that cast a cheerful orange glow on everyone's faces. Pim clung to her ankle. Torvald, the bard, had wrapped himself around the remaining rope like a koala and was still holding his lute, out of principle.

Above them, a dragon circled the cavern. It was enormous, red, and wreathed in smoke. It let out a roar that shook loose a few stalactites, and one of them plunged into the lava with a soft *plip*.

"Huh," said Pim. "That's new. The stalactite thing."

"Is it?" said Marguerite. "I feel like the Crypt of Whispers had a stalactite thing."

"That was stalagmites."

"Oh. Right."

The dragon dove. Everyone swung left in a practiced way, and a gout of flame passed harmlessly through the space where they'd been. The bridge creaked. Somewhere a pebble rolled.

"Can I say something?" said Torvald, muffled against the rope. "And I don't want this to come out wrong."

"Go ahead," said Dov.

"I'm a little bored."

There was a pause. The dragon wheeled around for another pass.

"Oh, thank the gods," said Pim. "I thought it was just me."

"It's not just you," said Marguerite. "I've been trying to figure out how to bring it up for weeks. I didn't want to be the one who killed the vibe."

"What vibe?" said Dov. "We're dangling over lava."

"Right, but we've dangled over lava *before*," said Marguerite. "That's my point. Three times this season. Four, if you count the volcano that was technically a hot spring."

"I don't count that one," said Pim. "I was wearing a robe. It was relaxing."

The dragon roared again, closer this time. Heat rolled across the bridge. Dov's eyebrows curled slightly.

"Okay, but the dragon's new," Dov offered.

"Is it, though?" said Torvald. "Red dragon, ancient, hoard of cursed gold, guards the artifact, tragic backstory we'll learn from a diary in the next room. Dov, we've fought that dragon. We fought it in the Ashen Peaks. We fought it in that other place with the bats."

"That one was *orange*."

"It was *sunset red*, Dov."

Dov opened his mouth, closed it, and shifted his grip on the rope. "Fine. Okay. Yes. The thing is, I really thought the dragon would be a bigger deal."

"Everyone did," said Pim. "That's what's so sad."

A fireball burst against the cavern wall and showered the group with sparks. Marguerite brushed an ember off her sleeve without looking.

"I miss the early days," she said. "Remember when we were first-level and a *goblin* could scare us? I once hid in a barrel for forty minutes."

"I remember," said Torvald fondly. "You wrote a song about that barrel."

"*You* wrote a song about that barrel."

"It was a good barrel."

"The point," said Dov, with the tone of a man trying to take back the conversation, "is that nothing surprises us anymore. We walk into a room, there's a trap, we say 'trap,' we do the thing with the pole. We walk into another room, there's a riddle, Pim does the riddle—"

"I'm very good at the riddles," said Pim.

"—and then there's a boss, and the boss has a *speech*, and we nod politely, and then we hit it until it falls over. I can't remember the last time I was truly scared."

"Last Thursday," said Torvald. "When the innkeeper charged us for the breakfast we hadn't ordered."

"That was a real fear," Dov agreed gravely. "That was a *real* fear."

The dragon landed on the far ledge, claws gouging the rock. It lowered its head until one enormous amber eye hung level with the dangling adventurers. Smoke curled from its nostrils.

"ARE YOU DONE?" it said.

Nobody answered right away.

"Sorry," said Marguerite. "Are we being rude? We can wait."

"I HAVE BEEN CIRCLING FOR FOUR MINUTES," said the dragon. "I HAVE ROARED SIX TIMES. YOU ARE SUPPOSED TO BE TERRIFIED."

"We're sort of terrified," said Pim, in a way that didn't help.

The dragon exhaled. It was a long, tired exhale, with only a little fire in it. "DO YOU KNOW," it said, "HOW MANY OF YOU I HAVE DONE THIS WITH?"

"Adventurers?" said Torvald.

"ADVENTURERS. HUNDREDS. EVERY ONE OF YOU WALKS IN WITH A SWORD AND A SPEECH AND A TRAGIC REASON. I GET UP, I DO THE ROAR, I DO THE FIRE. THEN THERE IS ALWAYS A BRIDGE. WHY IS THERE ALWAYS A BRIDGE?"

"I think the architect just really liked bridges," said Dov.

"THE ARCHITECT WAS ME," said the dragon. "I HAD A PHASE."

An awkward silence settled over the cavern, broken only by the distant bubbling of lava.

"Honestly?" said the dragon, a little more quietly. "I'M BORED TOO."

"Oh my gosh," said Pim.

"I HAVE HAD THE SAME HOARD FOR NINE HUNDRED YEARS. I KNOW EVERY COIN. THERE IS A GOBLET IN THERE I HAVE NEVER LIKED. I DO NOT KNOW WHY I KEEP IT."

"Have you thought about donating it?" said Marguerite.

"I HAVE NOT."

"You should. Think of the tax benefits."

"WHAT IS A TAX BENEFIT?"

"Honestly, I don't fully know," Marguerite admitted. "But people say it with a lot of confidence."

The dragon considered this. Then, with surprising delicacy, it reached out one claw and caught the frayed bridge rope. With a slow, careful pull, it hauled the whole sagging structure back toward the ledge, adventurers and all, and set them down on solid stone. Torvald unpeeled himself from the rope and kissed the ground.

"Thank you," said Dov, a little stiffly.

"DON'T MENTION IT," said the dragon. "SERIOUSLY. DON'T. IT WOULD RUIN MY REPUTATION."

They stood there for a moment, adventurers and dragon, in the orange glow, not quite sure what to do next.

"So," said Torvald. "Does anyone want to, like, get a drink?"

"I KNOW A PLACE," said the dragon, brightening. "IT IS A TAVERN. THE ONE NEAR THE OLD MILL. THE ALE IS TERRIBLE BUT THE PEOPLE ARE NICE. I CAN FIT IF I SIT IN THE YARD."

"Is it the one with the barrel out front?" said Marguerite.

"YES."

"Oh, I *love* that barrel."

They set out together, the dragon's tail sweeping the tunnel behind them, Pim already asking about the goblet and whether it was cursed, Torvald scribbling the first lines of a song.

"You know," Dov said to Marguerite as they walked, "I think that's the most surprised I've been in months."

"Same," said Marguerite. "Don't tell the others, but I'm a little excited about the next quest."

"Which is?"

"No idea. But I hear there's a bridge."

prompt: The time of Armageddon is soon . All the gods of various pantheons congregate to debate on why their end of the world should happen . While squabbling among each other , a god that was never worshiped speaks its mind .
content:
The hall had no walls, because no single pantheon could agree on whose architecture to use. So the gods sat in a ring on whatever they'd brought: Odin on a throne of ship timbers, Shiva on a tiger skin, an angel of the Seventh Trumpet on something that hummed. The Aztec Fifth Sun hung overhead and sulked, as he'd been told the lighting was his responsibility.

"Ragnarök," said Odin, for the ninth time, "has *structure*. Wolf, serpent, fire giant, the whole business. There is foreshadowing. There are *poems*."

"Revelation has seals," said the angel. "Seven. Seven trumpets, seven bowls. Yours has a *wolf*."

"Several wolves."

"Children," murmured Shiva, who had not opened his eyes in an hour. "The dissolution is cyclical. It will happen anyway. Why are we pretending to vote?"

"Because it's *our turn*," snapped Tezcatlipoca, from behind his smoking mirror. "The Fifth Sun ends in earthquakes. We were promised earthquakes. The Mayans had a date, and everyone *ignored* the date."

"The date passed," said Odin, "and nothing happened."

"That's what I'm *saying*. It was disrespectful."

The Zoroastrian delegation proposed a river of molten metal in which all souls would be purified, which drew a chorus of objections, mostly from the gods who had also proposed rivers of fire. The Hopi emissary pointed out that the Fourth World had already ended and wondered, mildly, whether anyone was keeping track. A minor Babylonian god was overheard saying that they'd done the flood first and nobody ever gave them credit. Someone's thunderbolt went off. Someone else's feelings were hurt.

It went on this way for what mortals would have measured as three weeks.

Then, from the far edge of the ring, where the light thinned out and the seating gave way to plain dark, a voice said, "May I?"

No one turned. Gods are not in the habit of turning toward the back.

"I'd like to say something," the voice repeated. It was neither deep nor loud. It sounded like a kettle starting to heat in another room.

Odin squinted. "Who is that?"

"I don't have a name," said the voice. "No one ever gave me one."

A silence spread through the ring, the kind that follows the discovery of a stranger at one's own family funeral.

"You're not on the list," said the angel, consulting a scroll.

"No. I wouldn't be."

The figure stepped into the light. It was difficult to describe, and later none of the gods agreed on what they'd seen. Some said it was a small gray-haired woman, and others a young man with sleep still in his eyes. To Shiva, who opened one eye, it looked like the moment just before a sunrise, when the sky has not yet decided on a color.

"What are you the god of?" asked Tezcatlipoca, not kindly.

"Mornings," said the figure. "Or, more precisely, *next*. The fact that there is a next. That the sun comes up, the bread rises, the child who went to sleep wakes up. The ordinary continuation. I suppose that's me."

Odin laughed, a short bark. "A god of *Tuesday*."

"Yes. If you like."

"And how many temples have they built you?"

"None."

"Prayers?"

"Not one."

"Then you can hardly speak for the mortals," said the angel, with satisfaction.

"I can't," the god agreed. "That's what I wanted to say. May I?"

No one said yes, but no one said no, and the gods had always been poor at telling the difference.

"You're all very good at being worshiped," the nameless god began. "I've watched you for a long time. I've had the time, since nobody ever asked me for anything. Odin, they prayed to you before battle, because they were afraid. Angel, they pray to you at deathbeds. Shiva, in the face of what can't be held. Tezcatlipoca, when the harvest failed. Every one of you was made out of a *worry*. A flood, a famine, the dark, the grave. People looked at the thing that frightened them and gave it a face so they could bargain with it."

"That is what gods are," said the angel stiffly.

"Yes. And I am what they never needed to bargain with. Because I've never failed them." The god's voice stayed mild. "Eleven billion mornings, give or take. Not one skipped. Not once did the sun fail to come up and the kettle fail to boil. And because I never failed, nobody noticed me. That's the only thing I've learned in all this time. *No one prays to what has never let them down.*"

Odin shifted on his throne. Nobody said anything.

"So I'll tell you what I think is happening in this room. You want the end because the end is the proof that you mattered. After the last battle, the last trumpet, the last turning of the wheel, somebody will say, *so the gods were real, and the stories were true.* You are afraid of the long quiet in which they stop telling the stories. You'd rather the world end *about* you than go on without you."

"That is a slander," said the angel, but his hum had gone unsteady.

"Is it?" The nameless god looked around the ring, and for the first time it seemed to look at each of them, one at a time, and every god felt it, like a hand on the shoulder. "Down there, right now, a woman is up before dawn to open a bakery. A boy is learning to tie his shoes. A man who hasn't spoken to his brother in nine years has picked up the phone and not yet dialed. None of them are praying. None of them need you for this. They're just *continuing*, the way I taught them without ever saying a word, and they'll keep doing it long after you've stopped arguing about which fire is the best fire."

"And what would you have us do?" Shiva asked softly. His eyes were fully open now.

"Nothing. That's the hard part." The nameless god almost smiled. "Let there be a morning that no one has to thank anyone for. Let some of you go on being loved a little less, or remembered only in the names of days and the shapes of old stories. That's not death. That's just being *finished*, the way a good meal is finished."

The hall was quiet for a long time.

Odin was the first to stand. He looked at the ship-timber throne as if seeing it for the first time, then at the small gray-and-gold figure at the edge of the light. "I had a very good wolf," he said, a little hoarsely.

"I'm sure you did."

"It would have been magnificent."

"I know."

One by one they left, not in anger but the way people leave a house after a long visit, lingering and gathering coats. The Fifth Sun drifted down toward the horizon, relieved to be off duty. The angel rolled up his scroll and, after hesitating, did not burn it. Tezcatlipoca's mirror cleared for a moment, and what it showed him was only a plain brown field, waiting for seed.

Shiva was the last. At the edge of the dark he paused and bowed his head to the nameless god, and it was the oldest bow in the world, the one given to the thing that was there before you arrived.

Then the hall was empty, and the nameless god stood alone.

Far below, a woman unlocked the door of a bakery. The oven ticked as it warmed. Through the window, the first gray light came up over the rooftops, as it always had.

The god watched it come, not needing to be thanked, and went to work.

content:
# The Engine Room

The *Halloran Belle* had one rule about the engine room: nobody went down there but Dessa Kowal.

So when the hatch clanged open at 3 a.m. and boots hit the ladder, she knew before she turned around that it wasn't one of the crew.

She was on her back under the number two generator with a wrench in her fist and a penlight in her teeth. She slid out slowly. Two men stood at the foot of the ladder. The big one had to stoop under the pipe run. The thin one was already looking past her at the locked steel cabinet bolted to the aft bulkhead.

"Evening," the thin one said. He raised his voice over the thrum of the diesels. "Captain says you have the key."

"Captain's asleep."

"Captain's tied to a chair," said the big one, not unkindly. "He's fine. For now."

Dessa stood up, and her knees popped. She was fifty-four. Behind the cabinet door were forty thousand dollars of someone else's money, which she had been stupid enough to agree to carry, and which the captain had been stupid enough to agree to hide. She had a bad shoulder and a worse hip, and the only weapon within reach was the wrench.

She did the math the way she did every math problem down here, quickly and without hope. Then she did it again with the room in it.

The room was her advantage. It was eleven feet wide, hot as a kiln, and loud enough that nobody upstairs would hear a thing. The deck plates were slick with a thin film of condensation and oil that she had stopped noticing years ago. The overhead was a maze of pipes, some lagged, some not. To her left, a four-inch steam line ran at waist height. Beside it was a gauge that she knew read a little low and a valve that she knew leaked.

"Tell you what," she said. "Let me get the key."

She reached for her belt, and the big one stepped forward to watch her hands.

That was her opening. She swung the wrench with her bad arm, a lazy, telegraphed arc. He caught it easily, the way she'd wanted, and closed his hand around the steel. She let go.

His eyes flicked down, confused for a quarter second, and she stamped hard on the inside of his knee.

It didn't break, but it buckled. He grunted and dropped half a foot, and she drove the heel of her hand up under his jaw. His head snapped back and cracked against a lagged pipe. It was soft insulation, so it didn't do much damage, but it stunned him. She tore her wrench out of his slackened grip and hit him across the forearm with it. Something gave with a wet little click, and he roared.

Then the thin man hit her.

She never saw it. A fist took her in the ribs, below the arm, exactly where it hurt most, and all the air left her. She folded. A knee came up into her face and she turned her head so it caught her brow instead of her nose. The world went white and bright. She tasted copper, and she hit the deck on her hands and knees.

*Get up. Get up, you stupid old woman. Up.*

A boot swung for her stomach. She didn't try to block it. She rolled into it, which robbed it of power, and grabbed the ankle and pulled. The thin man's other foot found the oily deck plate and skated. He went down hard on his tailbone and she heard his teeth click together.

She scrambled up. The room tilted and she used it, lunging for the one place she wanted to be, the steam line. The big man was already coming back, his arm hanging wrong and his face gone flat and patient. He wasn't angry anymore. That was worse.

He grabbed her by the collar and the belt and lifted her clean off the deck. She hit the bulkhead with her shoulder, the bad one, and her whole right side went to fire. She screamed. He pulled her back to throw her again.

She had one hand free, and it found the leaking valve.

She didn't think. She wrenched it open with everything she had left.

The steam came out of the cracked fitting in a white shriek, a scalding horizontal blade, and it caught the big man across the side of the face and neck. He let go of her and staggered away howling, both hands at his eyes. She dropped, slipped, and caught herself on the pipe rack. The burn from the pipe itself laid a stripe across her palm. She didn't let go. If she let go she'd fall, and if she fell she'd die.

The thin man was up. He had a knife now, short and ugly, and he was not talking anymore. He came in low and quick, and she did the only thing left, which was to make the room smaller. She hauled on the nearest hanging chain, and a ten-pound chain block swung down off its rail and clipped him across the shoulder. His slash went wide. The blade skidded along her ribs, and she felt the cold of it before the pain.

She hit him with the wrench.

It wasn't a clever swing. It was a mechanic's swing, a full arc from the hip, the kind she used on seized bolts. It caught him over the ear. He dropped without a sound and slid a foot across the oily deck, and the knife spun away under the generator.

Then the steam was the only noise, besides the diesels and her own ragged breath.

She limped to the valve and wrestled it shut with her good hand. The white cloud thinned. The big man was on his knees by the ladder, blinking with one eye, the other swollen shut and red. He looked at her, at the wrench, at his friend on the deck. He was a practical man. She saw him decide.

"Go up the ladder," Dessa said. Her voice came out a croak. "Cold water at the galley tap. Keep it on your face twenty minutes. Then go over the side, because I'm going to have the coast guard on the radio in ten."

"You're bleeding," he said.

"I've noticed."

He looked at her a moment longer, then climbed one-handed. The hatch rang above him.

Dessa stood very still until his boots faded. Then she sat down on the deck plates, carefully, with her back against the warm flank of the generator. She pressed her sleeve against her side and it came away dark but not terrible. She looked at the unconscious man, checked that his chest was rising, and kicked his knife farther away.

The cabinet door was still locked. The money was still inside.

She laughed, once, and it hurt, and she stopped.

After a while she took the penlight from where it had fallen and clicked it on. Then, because the number two generator still needed a gasket and nobody else on this boat could do it, she pulled herself up, wincing, and got back to work.

prompt: For as long as you can remember , you can hear background music appropriate to the situation you 're in . While going to the grocery store one day , you hear what sounds like the most generic JRPG battle theme you 've ever heard .
content:
For as long as I can remember, my life has had a soundtrack.

It's not a metaphor. When I was seven and my goldfish died, a lone cello followed me down the hallway. When I got my first kiss, a woodwind section I'd never asked for fluttered up from nowhere and then, mercifully, tactfully, faded out. At my grandmother's funeral there was only a soft, sustained piano chord, over and over, until I'd finished crying, and then it resolved. I've always been grateful for that one.

Mostly it's low-key. Library: hushed harp. Traffic: vaguely jaunty bass. The DMV: a single oboe, playing something that sounds like giving up.

The grocery store is usually smooth jazz, which I can easily tell apart from the store's own speakers, because mine has better production values.

So when I turned into the produce section on a Tuesday evening, holding a basket and a list that said *eggs, spinach, dish soap, something for dinner??*, and the music suddenly became *that*, I stopped dead beside the avocados.

It started with a screeching synth lead, followed by a double-kick drum pattern, and then strings sawed out a driving minor-key melody that I had heard a thousand times and never heard at all. It was every JRPG battle theme ever composed, boiled down into a paste. There was a key change at exactly the moment you'd expect one. A tambourine had no business being there, but it was there anyway.

I looked around for the danger.

A toddler was licking a cart handle. A man in a fleece vest was thumping melons with the gravity of a surgeon. Nobody was holding a weapon, and nobody was on fire.

"Hey! *Hey!* Is that Marcy Delgado?"

The strings jumped half a step, and I felt the drums in my sternum.

Across the apples, arms already spreading wide, came a woman in a blazer the color of a highlighter. It took me a moment, and then I knew her: Tricia Vanhoff, who sat behind me in eleventh-grade chemistry and once cried because I'd gotten a better grade on a titration lab.

**A wild Tricia appeared!** I did not hear that, exactly. I only felt it, the way you feel a sneeze coming.

"Oh my gosh, it's been *forever*," Tricia said. "You look amazing. Are you still at the same job? Do you ever feel like you're meant for more?"

The tambourine hit twice.

I knew this fight. I had lost this fight before, to a cousin, to a man at a wedding, and once, humiliatingly, to a teenager selling candy bars. I looked for options and found them rising in my mind like a menu: **Fight. Magic. Item. Run.**

I picked Run first, because I'm not an idiot. I took one casual step backward toward the bananas.

"Oh, don't go yet!" said Tricia, blocking the aisle with remarkable footwork. The music, which had been steady, seemed to chuckle and add a harmony line. *Can't escape!*

Fine.

I rummaged in my basket for an Item. I had eggs, a bag of spinach, and a bottle of dish soap. None of them seemed useful against a woman with a lanyard. I held up the spinach anyway, as a kind of shield, and Tricia said, "Oh! Do you juice?"

*It's not very effective.*

Magic, then. I don't have any. But years of living inside a soundtrack have taught me that the music wants things to resolve, to build and break and land. So I tried the thing that had always worked in the quiet moments, when I let the sound lead me. I took a breath and told the truth.

"Tricia, I'm really happy to see you, and I'm not going to join anything. But I'd love to hear how you've been. Really, how you've *been*."

The drums stuttered. The synth hung on a long, uncertain note.

Tricia blinked. The blazer, the lanyard, and the brightness all seemed to slip a little. "Oh," she said. "Um. Honestly? Not great. My husband left in March. I thought this would be..." She waved a hand at the lanyard as if it belonged to someone else. "I don't know. I don't really have anybody to talk to who isn't a *lead*."

The strings came down a whole octave, and the tambourine, bless it, fell silent.

We stood by the apples for twenty minutes. She told me about the divorce and the cat she was now raising alone, and I told her about the goldfish, for some reason, and she laughed so hard she had to hold on to the display. At the end she hugged me, and she did not try to sell me anything. She did ask for my number, but only for the normal reason.

The battle theme wound down into a bright, brassy fanfare, that little rising run of notes every gamer knows in their bones. It played all the way through, without embarrassment.

*Marcy gained 0 XP. Marcy gained a friend.*

I walked to the dairy aisle feeling about nine feet tall. Eggs. Spinach. Dish soap. I even found something for dinner, a rotisserie chicken still hot in its plastic dome, and I carried it to the front of the store like a trophy.

I scanned the eggs. I scanned the spinach. I scanned the dish soap and set it gently in the bagging area.

The self-checkout machine said, in a calm and terrible voice, "Unexpected item in the bagging area."

And from somewhere above the fluorescent lights, a choir began to sing in Latin.

I looked at the chicken. The chicken looked at me.

"Oh, come *on*," I whispered, as the pipe organ kicked in.

content:
# Last Orders

The recruiting posters never mentioned the paperwork.

They showed a necromancer in a dark greatcoat with one hand raised and a column of silver-eyed dead marching behind her, and they said SPECIAL DIVISION INFANTRY: THE DEAD DO NOT RETREAT. They did not show the card.

Every soldier in the Ninth Army carried one, folded behind the identity tags. It was called the Last Order, and it had three boxes. *Yes. No. Ask my family.* Sergeant Imre Valk had read hers ten thousand times, usually while someone's blood dried on her gloves.

Tonight she was counting boxes.

---

The bridge at Karsk was forty meters of stone over a gorge, and the Ninth Army's last two companies were still on the wrong side of it. Behind them the Verrish artillery had walked its fire up the valley all afternoon. Ahead of them, on the far bank, the engineers were wiring the span to blow, and they needed twenty minutes.

Imre had eleven living soldiers in her section, seventeen dead on the ground, and a cough she'd had since Tuesday.

"Sergeant." Corporal Dabney crouched beside her in the lee of an overturned supply cart. He was nineteen and looked twelve, and he had been trying not to look at the bodies for an hour. "Captain's orders. Hold the east approach for twenty minutes. Then fall back across."

"With what?"

Dabney didn't answer. His eyes went to the road, where the dead lay in rows. They had been laid out gently by the living, hands on chests, the way you did it before the necromancers came through.

Imre stood. Her knees cracked. She was thirty-four, and the work had put gray in her hair and a tremor in her left hand that wasn't from fear.

"Get me the cards," she said.

---

There were seventeen. She read each by the light of a shuttered lantern, with Dabney holding the box of tags.

*Pryce, Tomas. Yes.*
*Ibarra, Lucía. Yes.*
*Odum, Fenn. Yes.*
*Whitlock, Garrett. Ask my family.*

She set Whitlock's card aside. There was no time to ask a family. Fourteen more *Yes*. Then one more.

*Hadley, Mara. No.*

Imre stood looking at the card for a while. Mara Hadley had shared her tent for two years. She had taught Imre to play a dice game that Imre never won, and she'd died that afternoon with a piece of the Verrish shelling in her throat, in the first minute of the barrage. Imre had held her hand. Mara had mouthed something, and Imre had pretended to understand it.

*No.* In Mara's neat, square handwriting, with the pen pressed hard.

"Sergeant?" Dabney said quietly. "We're short. Fourteen's not enough for—"

"I know what it's enough for."

"I'm only saying, if—"

"Corporal." She did not raise her voice. "Mara said no. Nobody gets to say yes for her. Not you, not me, not the Captain, not the King. That's the whole point of the card. If we ignore it when we're desperate, it was never worth the ink."

Dabney swallowed and nodded.

Imre put Mara's card in her breast pocket, over her heart, and walked out to the road.

---

People imagined the work was grim and cold. It was warm. That was what the recruiters left out, and what the training cadre only admitted after you'd qualified.

You knelt and put your hands on the dead, and you gave them something. Not a spell exactly, but a loan of warmth, of will, of your own stubborn *being here*. The dead stood up on it. They fought on it. And the warmth came out of you, a little for each one, and some of it never came back.

Imre knelt by Tomas Pryce, a quartermaster's clerk who had cried at his own enlistment, and spoke the words every necromancer was taught. The words weren't magic. They were courtesy.

"Private Pryce. This is Sergeant Valk. You signed the card, and I'm honoring it. The line needs you for twenty minutes. After that, I'll let you go. You have my word."

His eyes opened silver. He stood. He picked up his rifle, and he looked like a man waiting to be told where to stand.

She did it fourteen times. By the ninth, her hands were numb. By the twelfth, she couldn't remember the name of the town where she'd grown up, and she noticed the gap only the way you notice a missing tooth. By the fourteenth, Dabney was holding her upright by the belt.

"You're done," he said.

"I'm not."

"Sergeant, you're gray."

"I'm *always* gray." She tried to smile. "Put me on the wall."

---

The Verrish came at the nineteenth minute, which was a minute earlier than the engineers had hoped and eleven minutes later than they'd feared.

Fourteen dead soldiers stood in the road in two ranks and did not break. Imre had watched this a hundred times and it still undid her: the way they fought without hatred, steady as a tide. They did not shout. Pryce, who had never fired anything but a ledger pen, stood in the front rank and took three rounds through the chest and kept loading. The Verrish vanguard slowed, then stopped, then began to fall back in confusion from an enemy that could not be frightened.

"Fall back!" the Captain's voice came across the gorge, thin with distance. "Section Valk, fall back across the bridge!"

The eleven living ran. Imre, kneeling in the road, did not.

"Sergeant!" Dabney had stopped halfway across.

"Go! I have to release them."

That was the other rule, the one the posters never showed. You could not leave them standing. A raised soldier left without release would keep fighting past the loan, past the bridge, past the end of the war, until the body fell apart, and nobody who'd done the work could stand the thought of that. You laid them down yourself.

She walked down the line with her hand out. At each one she stopped.

"Private Ibarra. Thank you. You're released."

Ibarra's silver eyes dimmed to brown and she sank gently to the road, hands crossed, as if she'd only been sleeping.

"Private Odum. Thank you. You're released."

Fourteen times. Her voice cracked on the ninth and she kept going. Behind her the Verrish were regrouping. She could hear the whistle of the first shells finding their range again.

At the last she came to Pryce, still in the front rank with his rifle level, a dozen holes in his coat.

"Private Pryce. You held the line. You held it very well." She found, absurdly, that she was crying. "You're released."

He lowered the rifle and looked at her. For one moment, though she would never be sure and never tell anyone, his eyes were not silver at all.

"Thank you, Sergeant," he said.

Then he lay down.

---

She made the bridge with nine seconds to spare, running on legs that belonged to someone else. Dabney caught her at the far end and half-dragged her behind the sandbags as the engineers threw the charge.

The span went up in a flat white roar. Stone and smoke boiled into the gorge. When it cleared there was only air between the banks, and the Verrish standing on the far side with nothing to cross.

Imre sat in the dirt and took the folded card out of her pocket. The paper was soft from handling, the ink a little smeared by her thumb.

*Hadley, Mara. No.*

"She'd have been the best one," Dabney said hesitantly. "Wouldn't she? Best fighter in the section."

"Yes."

"Do you ever wish—"

"Every time." She smoothed the card flat on her knee. "That's why it's *her* box to check, and not mine."

Across the gorge, the smoke thinned. Somewhere in it lay fourteen soldiers who had been asked, and had answered, and had been thanked. Beside them lay one who had been asked and had said no, and had been believed.

Imre folded the card along its old crease, tucked it back over her heart, and closed her eyes. For a moment she couldn't remember her hometown, or her mother's face, or what Mara had mouthed in that last minute. But she remembered the dice game. She remembered the rules. She remembered that she'd never once won.

It would do, she thought. It would have to.

"Sergeant?" Dabney said softly.

"I'm here," said Imre Valk, Special Division Infantry, Necromancer Class. "I'm still here."

content:
# Przedwiośnie

Death arrived at sunrise, as was the old courtesy, and knocked, which he rarely bothered to do.

The woman who opened the door was small and seventy-nine, in a cardigan buttoned one hole off. A gray cat wound around her ankles. She looked at him for a long moment, at the dark coat and the stillness that sat on him like frost on a windowpane, and said, "Oh. It's today."

"It's today," said Death.

"You're early."

"I'm not. The appointment is at eleven forty-seven tonight. I'm only here because it's polite to be present."

"Polite." She seemed to like that. "Well, come in, then. I'm not going to make you stand on the step all day. Do you drink tea?"

He had been asked many things over the ages. *Please. Not yet. Who will feed the dog. Are you my mother.* No one had ever asked him that.

"I don't know," he said.

"Then we'll find out."

---

Her name was Ines Albrecht, and she had spent fifty years translating other people's poems into English. The kitchen was lined with dictionaries, their spines gone soft as old fruit. Death sat at a table that had known a great many breakfasts and held a cup he did not know how to hold. The steam touched his face. He found it interesting.

"Well?" said Ines.

He sipped. "It's hot."

"That's the idea."

"It tastes like..." He searched for it. "Like a room someone has just left. Still warm."

Ines stared at him, then laughed, a short surprised bark. "That's the best review that tea has ever gotten."

She did not weep or bargain. She said she'd done her weeping in March, when the doctor gave her the shape of things, and had made her peace the way you make a bed, tucking in the corners. She had only one problem left, and it was a line.

---

The line sat in the study, on a desk buried under paper. She was translating a Polish poet, long dead, a slim book that had never been put into English. Everything was finished but one poem, and in that poem, one word.

"*Przedwiośnie*," she said. "It means the time before spring. Not winter, and not spring either. The weeks when the ground is mud and the branches are bare, but something has started under all of it. English has no word. 'Early spring' is a lie, because it's not spring. 'Late winter' is a lie too. I've tried forty things." She waved at a wastebasket full of them. "I wanted to leave it right. It seems a small thing to want."

Death read the poem. He read it standing, with his hands behind his back. He knew something about thresholds. He had spent all of time on them, in the long gray hallway between what was and what wasn't, and he knew its particular light.

"You're translating it as a season," he said. "It isn't one. The poet is describing a kind of waiting that has already begun to be the thing it waits for."

Ines went very still. "Say that again."

He said it again. She wrote it down and then crossed it out and wrote something else, her pen scratching. Outside the morning went on and became afternoon. Death found that he did not want to look at the clock, and he had never before had a wish about time.

---

They ate at one o'clock, bread and a hard cheese. She asked what he did with the hours when he wasn't working, and he said there weren't any, not the way she meant. He was always at every ending at once, a long ache of arrivals. He was at a hospital in Lagos and a ditch in a country whose name was changing and a bed in this very town where an old man was already, quietly, beginning to go.

"That sounds lonely," she said.

"It isn't anything. It's what I am."

"That's what lonely is, dear. Not having a word for it because it's the weather you live in."

He had no answer. He turned the cup in his hands.

She told him about her husband, Tomasz, dead eleven years, who couldn't cook and had once set fire to a salad. She told him about the cat, which had been a stray with half an ear, and about the winter in Kraków when she was twenty-six and learned the language by reading gravestones. He listened the way he had never listened to anyone, without his mind already reaching for the end of the sentence. He knew the end of every sentence. But he had never stayed for the middle of one.

Somewhere past four in the afternoon, with light coming low and gold through the kitchen window, he understood what was happening to him. It arrived the way the tea had, a warmth he didn't have a place to put.

*Oh,* he thought. *Oh, no.*

---

"You've gone quiet," she said at dusk.

"I'm considering something I shouldn't."

"You could take me now," she said gently. "If it would be easier. I won't mind."

"That's not it." He looked at her, at the one misbuttoned hole, the ink on her thumb, the stubborn soft face. "It would be easier to take you now. That's the trouble. I've never wanted to be slow before."

She was quiet. The cat jumped into her lap, and she stroked it without looking down.

"Ah," she said. "I see."

"I'm sorry. It's absurd. You're a day's acquaintance, and I'm..."

"Don't you dare apologize." Her voice had a crack in it, but it was not grief. It was something nearer to delight. "Seventy-nine years old, and Death is sitting in my kitchen with a crush. Do you know how many people would give anything for a story like that?"

"I can't change the hour."

"I know."

"I can't keep you."

"I know that too." She reached across the table and set her hand over his. It was the first time anyone had touched him on purpose. Her skin was papery and very warm. "I'm not asking you to. I'm only glad it's you. I'd been afraid it would be someone who didn't care."

---

At eleven they went back to the study. She read him the finished poem aloud, and in the place where the word had been she had left a line that was not a word at all but a small, precise phrase: *the season that has already started to be spring.* She said it wasn't perfect. He said it was right.

At eleven forty she sat in her armchair with the cat and a blanket. He knelt beside her, which he had never done for anyone.

"Will it hurt?" she asked, not frightened, only curious, the way she'd asked about the tea.

"No. It will be like..." He thought of the word she had found. "Like the last of the winter. And then something already under it."

"*Przedwiośnie,*" said Ines, and smiled.

"Yes."

"What's your name? I should have asked this morning."

"I don't have one."

"Everyone has one." She considered him, her eyes bright and wet. "Then I'll keep it simple. Thank you for the tea, whoever you are."

At eleven forty-seven the clock in the hall ticked once, and he took her hand, and she went through the door that is not a door, easily, the way a person steps out of a warm house into the first mild night of the year. She turned once on the threshold and touched his cheek, a brief dry kiss like a leaf landing. Then the light took her, and she was past where he could follow.

He stayed kneeling in the study a long time.

---

Death had walked the edge of every life for as long as there had been lives, and he had never been left behind. He learned it that night in the quiet house, with a gray cat watching him from the armchair and the poem lying finished on the desk. He understood, finally, what the living carried all their short years. It was heavy. It was also, he thought, the most beautiful thing he'd ever been handed.

At dawn he rose. There was a man in a hospital bed across town, nearly at the end, whose daughter was asleep in the chair beside him. The call was coming. It was always coming.

But this time Death went early, and he knocked. He sat down by the bed and said softly, to the man and to the sleeping girl and to the long gray light, "I'm in no hurry. Tell me about her."

And he listened to the middle of the sentence.

content:
# The Ferry at Karsk

The magazine called it "The Face Project." Twelve months, twelve countries, and one photograph at the end that would, in the editor's words, "settle the question forever." I was hired because I was good at light, and because I had once been quoted saying that beauty was a solvable problem.

By the eleventh month I had photographed an actress in Seoul whose cheekbones had their own insurance policy, a Somali-Norwegian model who could stop traffic by tying her shoes, and a Brazilian schoolteacher whose beauty was so uncomplicated that I felt rude pointing a lens at it. All of them were extraordinary. None of them settled anything. I'd look at the contact sheets and feel what you feel when you read a word too many times and it stops meaning itself.

The twelfth country was a formality. A cousin of the Karsk regional governor had written to the magazine insisting that the most beautiful woman in the world ran the river ferry in a town no one had heard of. The editor wanted to include one "discovery," and I was already in the region, so I rented a car that smelled of wet dogs and drove for six hours into the hills.

---

The river at Karsk is wide and brown and moves slowly, as if it has somewhere to be but has decided not to rush. The ferry was a flat steel barge with a rope-and-pulley system, and a woman stood at the front of it, coiling a line.

She was perhaps sixty. Her face was square and weathered, her nose had been broken at some point and set a little to the left, and her gray hair was stuffed under a man's wool cap. She wore rubber boots and a coat that had been mended in at least three different colors of thread.

"You're the photographer," she said. It wasn't a question. "The governor's cousin told everyone. Half the town wanted to dress up. I told them you'd want the river, not the dress."

"I was told I'd be photographing the most beautiful woman in the world."

"Then you were lied to." She said it cheerfully, hauling on the rope. "Get in the car if you're crossing. Otherwise you're in my way."

I drove onto the barge. I told myself I'd take a few frames, file the assignment under *rural color*, and be back in the capital by the weekend.

---

Her name was Ines. She had run the ferry for thirty-one years, since her father's hands gave out. She crossed the river forty times a day in summer, fewer in winter, when the ice came in plates and she had to go out first with a pole.

I shot her the way I'd shot the others, with careful light and a long lens, asking her to look left, to look at the water, to *think of something happy.* She did all of it patiently, the way you'd humor a child who wants to play a game. The frames were competent. They showed a tired, plain woman looking at a river.

"You're disappointed," she said, around the fourth crossing.

"No."

"You are. It's all right. The governor's cousin is half blind and fully in love with me, which is a different thing than beauty. I've told him."

I laughed. It surprised me. "In love with you?"

"Since 1989. He proposes every spring when the ice breaks. It's a kind of weather."

---

I stayed for three days. I told myself it was for the light.

What I actually did was watch. A boy with a crate of ducks came aboard, and Ines, without breaking her stride, lifted one duck out, checked its eye, handed it back, and said, "That one's sick. Keep it from the others." A man who had clearly been drinking since morning tried to pay with a coin from a country that no longer existed, and she took it, turned it over, and said, "Good, I've been missing one of these," and let him board for free. She never said anything to spare his feelings, but his shoulders came down anyway.

On the second evening, a woman came to the landing with a coffin-shaped box strapped to a cart. Nobody said what was in it. The woman stood with her hands knotted together, and Ines stopped the engine in the middle of the river, which I learned later she was not supposed to do, and let the barge drift in the slow brown current for ten minutes. She didn't speak. She stood at the rail with her cap in her hands. Then she started the engine again and delivered them to the far bank, and the woman pressed something into her palm, and Ines pressed it back.

I had my camera up. I didn't take the shot. For the first time in twelve months I understood that the shutter would have been a kind of theft.

---

The thing I'd gotten wrong, I think, was that I'd been treating beauty as a property of faces: something you could locate, measure, and rank. But what I'd watched in Karsk was something that happened *in time.* It was a way of paying attention that moved through a person and out into the world, so that the world, briefly, was arranged better for her having passed through it. The sick duck. The coin. The ten minutes of drifting.

You can't photograph that, or not directly. A photograph is a thousandth of a second, and what I'd seen took days.

On the last morning, I found her at the front of the barge, hauling the rope hand over hand against the current. Her hands were enormous and scarred, the knuckles swollen, the nails cracked short. The rope ran through them as if they'd been designed for it, as if the river and the rope and the hands were all one sentence that had been finished a long time ago.

I took one picture. Just her hands on the wet rope, the brown water behind, a smear of morning light along the knuckles. No face at all.

---

The editor hated it, of course. "Where's the woman?" she asked. "The whole point is the woman."

"That is the woman," I said.

We argued for an hour. In the end the issue ran with eleven faces, all breathtaking, and one pair of hands on a rope. Beneath the hands, in small type, was the caption I had insisted on: *Ines, ferry operator, Karsk. Thirty-one years.* The editor added a subheading of her own: *Beauty, Unretouched.* I let her. It wasn't quite right, but it wasn't quite wrong either.

I mailed a copy to the governor's cousin, with a note asking him to read it to her. I never found out if he did. Months later, a package arrived at my studio containing a coin from a country that no longer existed, and a piece of paper that said, in blunt capital letters:

*YOU GOT THE LIGHT RIGHT. COME BACK WHEN THE ICE BREAKS. HE WILL PROPOSE AGAIN. I WANT A WITNESS.*

I went. She turned him down again, kindly, and the ice went out on the river with a sound like a long breath, and for one hour that afternoon I stood on the landing with my camera hanging forgotten at my side, and watched the most beautiful woman in the world coil a rope.

content:
# The Epilogue

They took me outside a laundromat in Duluth. Someone put a hand over my mouth, and the hand smelled faintly of tar and lemon oil. When I woke up I was in a cabin that creaked, though the floor beneath me was perfectly still. Later I learned they had built the cabin inside a drained grain silo, with the walls curved and the lamps swinging on chains. The creaking came from a speaker hidden in the ceiling.

A man sat across from me in a chair bolted to the floor. He was sixty or so, bearded and weathered, with a gentle, professorial face. He wore a peacoat and held a paperback so worn that its spine had gone soft as cloth.

"You're awake," he said. "Good. I hate to start a voyage with a late sleeper."

"Where am I?"

"Where is anyone?" he said, smiling. "But I take your meaning. You're aboard the *Pequod*. She's a silo for now, but we're not particular about hulls. The book makes clear that a ship is mostly an agreement."

"The book," I said.

He held it up. The cover was the old orange Penguin edition, and the title was nearly rubbed away. "You wrote a piece about us," he said. "'Lake County Cult Worships Whale Book.' Three hundred words in the Metro section. You called us 'a harmless group of eccentrics obsessed with a very long novel.'"

"I was told it was harmless."

"It was accurate, if reductive. Most things are." He leaned forward. "You may call me Captain. I know how it sounds. We tried 'Reverend,' but it felt like a costume, and a captain at least has duties. There are forty-one of us. We've read *Moby-Dick* aloud, cover to cover, every year for nineteen years, beginning on the first of October. It takes eleven days if no one gets sick. Once a man had a stroke at 'The Whiteness of the Whale,' and we finished the chapter before we called anyone. He would have wanted that."

"What do you want with me?"

He opened the book to a place marked with a pressed flower and read in a low, practiced voice: "'*And I only am escaped alone to tell thee.*'"

The silo creaked and the lamps swayed.

"It's the Epilogue," he said. "It's also the Book of Job, which Melville borrowed it from, but we don't make a fuss about that. Here is the heart of our understanding, and you're a professional, so you'll appreciate it. The novel is not a story about a whale. It's a story about a *witness*. Ahab doesn't matter, and neither does the whale, and the crew least of all. The crew exist to be lost. The whole terrible machine of the book runs so that one man can be left on the water, and the only reason to leave him there is so that the story will exist. Without Ishmael there's no book. There's only a ship that went out and didn't come back, which happens every day and means nothing."

"You're going to sink a ship," I said.

"We're going to *complete* one." He said it kindly. "Nineteen years we've been preparing. The Great Lakes are not the Pacific, but Superior has her own opinions, and in November she shares them freely. We've bought a forty-foot trawler and renamed her. We've forged an iron harpoon. Brother Dennis, who was an orthodontist, has been working on a prosthetic leg of whalebone, though we've had to settle for polymer. And on the fourth of November, in weather the Coast Guard will call unwise, we'll go out after a thing none of us has seen."

"There's no white whale in Lake Superior."

"No," he agreed. "That's what makes it a *faith*."

I tried the restraints on my wrists. They were soft rope, properly knotted, and that was somehow worse.

"Everyone aboard has a part," the Captain went on. "Brother Dennis will be Starbuck, because he doubts. Sister Ruth will be Pip, and I won't say more about that. We have a Queequeg, a retired welder from Hibbing, a very quiet man who has asked to be tattooed, and I told him, 'Gerald, we'll see.' I will be Ahab. I've never asked anyone else to be Ahab. It's a terrible thing to want, and I want it a great deal, and I think that's the qualification."

"And I'm Ishmael."

He looked almost tender. "You see it. I knew you would. You write for a living, and you wrote us up as a joke, which means you were paying attention. Ishmael isn't a hero. He's a schoolteacher who goes to sea because he's low in spirits, and he's the only one who looks at the whole thing and thinks, *I should put this down.* We tried to find one of our own for the role. But every one of us wants to be the whale or the captain. No one wants to be the man who watches. It turns out that's the rarest vocation there is."

"You're going to drown forty people to get a book."

"We're going to drown forty people to get a *Gospel*," he said. "Think of it. Every scripture was written by someone who came back. Every one has a survivor in the last chapter. We don't have one. We have a book about a survivor, which is only the shadow of the thing, and we've been living in the shadow for nineteen years. We'd like to have the real article for once."

He stood, took a key from his pocket, and walked to a tarp on the far wall. He pulled it away.

It was a coffin of pale cedar, beautifully made, with rope handles at the sides and a lid sealed with pitch. Carved into the lid in careful capitals was a single word, and the word was not my name. It was blank, a smooth oval of wood where a name would go.

"Queequeg built his own when he thought he was dying," the Captain said. "Then he recovered, and the coffin became the life-buoy that saved Ishmael. It's the strangest and most merciful thing in American literature. The thing built for death becomes the thing that carries you through it. We've tested ours in the lake. It floats. It rides a little low, but it floats." He laid a hand on the lid. "Brother Gerald made it. He wept the whole time."

My voice came out smaller than I wanted. "And if I refuse? If I don't write it?"

"Oh," said the Captain, and for the first time he looked a little sad. "But you will. You'll float for a day and a night, and you'll be picked up by a ship called the *Rachel*, or something as good. We've arranged that, too. Sister Ruth's nephew has a charter boat. And then you'll sit in a hospital with a blanket on your shoulders, and a policeman will ask what happened, and you'll find you can't stop. You'll tell it again and again, and each time it will get a little more shapely. Don't be ashamed. It isn't weakness. It's the thing you are."

He returned to his chair and sat, and the lamps swung gently over his face.

"We don't ask you to believe," he said. "Ishmael doesn't believe, you know. He's the only one aboard who doesn't. He just *goes*. He signs on and he looks and he stays alive. I think that's the whole of the Gospel, really."

"What do I call you? In the book?"

He brightened, and I saw that this was the question he had been waiting for. It was what he'd wanted from me from the beginning, and I had given it to him.

"Whatever you like," he said. "That's the privilege. You're the author now."

He handed me the paperback, and the spine fell open to the first page, where someone had long ago pencilled a margin note in a small, careful hand. The note said: *begin here.*

The speaker in the ceiling creaked, and somewhere above me a rope, or the idea of one, drew taut.

I read the first line to myself, because I couldn't help it.

Then I thought, with a clarity that frightened me far more than the coffin did: *I would change the second sentence.*

The Captain was watching my face. He nodded slowly, as a man nods when a sail finally fills.

"There," he said. "You see? You've already started."

content:
# The Hall of Terrestrials

Curator Ixh-of-the-Seventh-Tide had four hours before the first living human walked into the museum, and the humans were still wrong.

"Not wrong," said her assistant, tapping a tendril against the display rail. "Interpreted."

"Wrong," said Ixh, "is an interpretation that has met its subject."

She walked the length of the hall once more. A hundred years of guessing lay on either side of her, collected from a dozen worlds, each depicting the same small, wet, loud species from a distance of many light-years.

---

**The first exhibit** was from the Veshti, who have no eyes and see by vibration. They had caught the early radio leakage and rendered it as sound-sculpture: a tall lattice of humming glass that shivered when you approached. The placard read:

*THOSE WHO HUM. Terrestrials are beings of pure pattern, made of music and static. They speak constantly, mostly to announce what the sky will do. Their most sacred rite is the Weather Report, performed at regular intervals, in which a single priest stands before a map and tells the future with great confidence and frequent error. The Veshti revere them for their humility.*

Ixh had always liked this one. It was not true, but the lattice sang a low, lovely chord when the air moved through it. The humans, she suspected, would claim they had meant to do that.

---

**The second exhibit** came from the Orrin, a hive-minded people who cannot imagine a mind without a body to share it. Theirs was a vast, tangled sculpture of eight billion threads knotted into one slumped shape.

*THE GREAT ANIMAL. Terrestrials are a single organism distributed across many bodies. The organism is gravely ill. Its limbs fight one another. Its left hand strikes its right and then writes poems about the bruise. Orrin physicians have prescribed rest, cooperation, and the immediate cessation of "Tuesday." We do not know what Tuesday is. It appears to be the source of the trouble.*

Ixh had added a small note beneath it: *Treatment ongoing. Prognosis uncertain. Patient shows flashes of surprising vigor.*

---

**The third exhibit** was her favorite and the one she was least sure she should have hung. It came from a planet that had intercepted only one thing, a golden disc some humans had flung into the dark decades ago. The sculptors of that world had studied it with the devotion of monks. They had a naked pair of figures with raised hands, a diagram of a hydrogen atom, and fifty-five greetings in fifty-five tongues. From these they built a portrait of a people who were unfailingly, almost unbearably polite.

*THE GREETERS. Terrestrials exist in a perpetual state of welcome. They meet one another, and all things, with a raised hand and a kind word. They are fond of whales. They have never had a bad day. When one dies, the others play a piece of music by a man named Chuck, and all is forgiven.*

"They'll hate that one," said the assistant.

"They'll weep at that one," said Ixh. "It's the most flattering lie in the building."

---

**The fourth exhibit** was a small clay tablet, almost an afterthought, made by the children of a colony world who had received only a stream of what the humans called *entertainment*. Their rendering showed a large, soft figure bent low before a small furred one seated on a throne.

*HUMANS. They serve the Cats. The Cats do not appear to notice. The humans seem happy.*

Ixh had tried to retire this tablet twice. Both times the schoolchildren of three systems had written to protest. She had decided that the children knew something she did not.

---

**The last exhibit** stood at the end of the hall under a plain white light. It was the oldest, and it came from the Kal.

The Kal live for thirty thousand years, and to them a human life is the flicker of a struck match. They had built no figure at all, only a single flame in a glass dome, burning steadily, tended by a Kal volunteer who replaced it each time it guttered. The placard was short.

*THE BRIEF. We have watched them for what, to them, is a thousand generations, and to us has been one long afternoon. They are born, they blaze, they are gone, and in the instant of their burning they build cathedrals, write symphonies, split the atom, and leave one another notes. We do not understand how so much can be made by so little time. We have stopped trying to understand. We simply keep the light on.*

Ixh stood before it for a long moment. Every other exhibit in the hall was a mistake. This one was only incomplete.

---

The door chimed. The human delegate had arrived early.

She was smaller than Ixh had imagined, with gray hair and a lanyard and a tired, curious face. She carried a translation device and a paper cup of something steaming. She stopped at the entrance of the Hall and looked down the long row of exhibits.

She walked past the Veshti lattice and laughed out loud when it hummed at her. She stood a long time before the Orrin sculpture, and her smile went crooked. "Yeah," she said quietly. "That's fair."

At the Greeters she covered her mouth. At the clay tablet of the Cats she laughed so hard she had to set down her cup. "Oh, they're *right*," she gasped. "Oh, my God, they're so right."

Then she came to the end of the hall and the small flame in its dome. She read the placard twice. The laughter went out of her face, but something warmer replaced it.

"Who made this?" she asked.

"The Kal," said Ixh. "They are very old. They were not sure you would want it displayed."

"Why not?"

"It is not funny," said Ixh. "The others are funny. We worried this one might be... true."

The human was quiet. The flame bent a little in some draft Ixh could not feel, then straightened again.

"We got a lot wrong about you, too," the human said at last. "We thought you'd be bigger. Or meaner. We drew you with a lot of tentacles." She glanced at Ixh's tendrils. "Okay, we got the tentacles right." She smiled. "But we spent a hundred years sending messages into the dark, and we never knew if anyone was reading. We figured if anyone was, they'd get us completely wrong."

"We did," said Ixh.

"Yeah." The human looked back down the long hall of lattices and knots and clay, at every strange, loving, mistaken portrait of her people. "But you *looked*. Nobody told you to. You just kept looking and kept guessing, and you built all this." She gestured at the glass, the sculpture, the small steady flame. "That's more than we ever hoped for."

Ixh did not know the human custom for such a moment, so she improvised. She raised one tendril in the air, the way the golden disc had shown, and held it there.

The human raised her hand in return.

Behind them, in its glass dome, the little flame went on burning.

prompt: You caused the home team to lose the big game due to an absurd chain reaction that started from your seat in the crowd . No one knows exactly what happened except for you .
content:
# Section 114, Row 8, Seat 12

Let me say up front that I did not mean to do it, and that nobody will ever believe me, which is the only reason I'm still able to walk around this city.

It was Game 7. Bottom of the ninth had been a formality, because we were the home team and we were already ahead, 4–3. The Gulls had waited thirty-one years for this. The man next to me had a tattoo of the 1993 roster on his calf, and he was openly weeping into a pretzel.

Top of the ninth. Two outs. Two strikes on the batter. Our closer, Marcus "The Lighthouse" Odell, was one pitch from immortality.

This is when I made my mistake, which was ordering the Stadium Supreme Nachos with extra jalapeños.

---

I'd been saving the last chip for the final out. It was the perfect chip, loaded with a molten cap of cheese and one lone jalapeño ring on top. I lifted it to my mouth as Odell began his windup, and the pepper dust found my nose.

I'd like to say I fought the sneeze. I did not. It came up from somewhere ancestral.

The chip left my hand like a missile.

It struck Dennis, the man in front of me, directly between the shoulder blades. I know his name was Dennis because it was on his jersey, and also because I learned it later, in the worst way. Dennis yelped and flung his arms forward, and his full beer, a sixteen-ounce domestic, went up and over his head and onto the woman in the row below.

She rose like a Pentecostal. She screamed, "MY HAIR!" and swung around with her giant foam finger, which caught a vendor's tray. The vendor was a teenager named Kyle, and Kyle was carrying nine hot dogs and a stack of those little cardboard boats.

Eight of the hot dogs stayed on the tray. One did not.

It arced out over the railing, turning end over end in the stadium lights, and landed in the first-row aisle with a soft *thap*, in full view of the sky.

I want to be clear that nobody else saw this. Sixty thousand people were watching Marcus Odell. I was watching a hot dog.

---

The Gulls, the real ones, are an urban menace, and our stadium has them in abundance. There was one, enormous and gray-backed and mean, that had been circling the upper deck all night like a tiny feathered bomber.

It saw the hot dog.

I watched it fold its wings and dive. It came down over the third-deck overhang, past the foul pole and over the heads of the whole first section, a gull on a mission. It grabbed the hot dog off the concrete without even slowing, banked left with its prize, and sailed out over the field.

Odell was in the middle of his delivery.

I will never forget his face. The gull crossed his sightline at about head height, trailing a bun, six feet from his ear, and Marcus Odell, a man who had faced down the best hitters in the world, flinched.

The pitch left his hand sideways. It sailed in at the batter's ribs, and the batter, a veteran named Ruiz, turned into it so gracefully that I suspect he'd been waiting his whole career for a gull to do him this favor.

*Hit by pitch.* Runner on first.

The gull, for the record, landed on the outfield grass and finished the hot dog in peace.

---

The next batter was their cleanup man, a mountain named Beltrán. Odell was rattled and the crowd was confused. Somebody in the upper deck was shouting about the bird, and a general murmur went up, the sound of sixty thousand people trying to decide whether they'd just seen something or not.

Odell's next pitch was a fastball that was supposed to be on the outside corner. It was not on the outside corner. It was in the middle of the plate, at the belt, announcing itself.

The sound that Beltrán's bat made is the sound I hear when I close my eyes at night.

The ball went out to left-center and kept going. It cleared the wall, the bullpen, and what I think was a beer garden. A two-run homer.

5–4, visitors.

Our stadium, which had been a single roaring organism for three hours, went silent. Dennis turned slowly around, nacho cheese drying on his jersey, and looked straight at me with the dead eyes of a man who has lost something he'll never get back.

"Did you see that *bird*?" he whispered.

"Yeah," I said. "Crazy."

---

We went down in order in the bottom of the ninth. Three batters, nine pitches. I barely remember it. I was busy being a ghost.

The postmortems were brutal. Sports radio blamed Odell's nerves. One columnist called it "the Gull Game" and described the bird as "a cruel omen," and a man on TV said the baseball gods had a sense of humor. A petition went up to have the stadium's gulls "relocated." The mayor commented. Dennis was interviewed outside the ballpark, looking haunted, and said, "It was just one of those things. Nobody could've seen it coming."

I was standing right behind him in the shot, holding a cardboard tray with one soggy chip on it.

---

I've thought about confessing. I've drafted the letter. *To the people of Gull City: it was a chip. It was a jalapeño chip. I'm so sorry.* But what good would it do? Thirty-one years of waiting, undone by a sneeze, and I'd be the face of it forever. They'd put me on a mural. A bad one.

So I keep it to myself. I go to work, I nod when people bring it up at parties, and I say, "Brutal," and, "That bird, man," and I let them blame fate, because fate can handle it.

Next season, though, I got my tickets again. Same section, same row, same seat. I told myself it was for closure.

Top of the ninth, up two runs, I ordered a pretzel. Plain. No cheese, no peppers, nothing airborne.

Dennis was two rows down. He turned, saw me, and squinted.

"Hey," he said slowly. "Don't you sit here every game?"

"Just the important ones," I said.

He nodded, satisfied, and turned back around.

Above us, in the lights, something gray and enormous began to circle.

I held my pretzel very, very tightly.

prompt: In a world where simulations have become the norm , it gets increasingly difficult to tell the difference between simulation and reality . You 've just met the girl of your dreams , literally . Only thing is you ca n't tell if she 's real or a figment if the simulation .
content:
# The Seam

The Disclosure Act says every simulation must answer truthfully if you ask whether it is one. Everyone knows the law, and everyone knows about the black-market builds that lie.

So the first thing I said to Wren, on a pier that smelled like salt and diesel, was, "Are you real?"

She didn't look up from the knot she was tying in a length of rope. "That's a terrible opener."

"It's the law."

"The law says *I* have to answer *you*. It doesn't say I have to enjoy it." She pulled the knot tight and met my eyes. They were gray-green, with a fleck of brown in the left one, the kind of flaw a designer would never add on purpose, which meant a good designer would add it on purpose. "Yes. I'm real. Are you?"

That was three weeks ago, and I haven't stopped thinking about it.

---

I rent my sleep, like most people. Nobody has dreams anymore. They have *Lulls*, eight-hour curated sessions piped straight into the hindbrain, with better lighting than anything your own head could manage. I'd been renting a harbor town called Marrow Bay for two years. I knew its streets, and I knew its fishmonger was a loop with forty-one lines of dialogue.

Wren wasn't one of the forty-one lines.

She showed up on a Tuesday, sitting on the end of the pier with her boots dangling over the water. When I sat down beside her, she said, "You're the guy who always walks to the lighthouse and never goes in."

"It's locked."

"It's not. You've just never tried the door."

I tried the door. It opened, which was wrong. For two years that door had been a painted-on prop. Inside there was a spiral staircase and a lamp room, and she'd already been up there, apparently, because there was a thermos of real-tasting tea waiting on the sill.

Here was the problem. Either she was a user who'd found a hidden-room exploit and wandered into my private Lull, which shouldn't be possible, or she was something the Bay had grown to keep me company. The platforms do that now. They watch what makes you linger, and then they build it.

I didn't know which was worse: that she might be a product, or that I wouldn't mind.

---

For three weeks I ran tests, and I'm not proud of them.

I counted her fingers. Always five. I asked her to read a line of text, look away, and read it again, because old sims garbled words the second time. She read it perfectly both times and then told me I was being a creep.

I asked about things I thought no designer would bother with. What's the worst thing you ate as a child? ("Canned peaches. My uncle kept them in the garage through a flood. They tasted like the garage.") What do you do when you can't sleep? ("Sleep is not my problem. *Waking* is. Nothing is ever as good as the Bay.") What's the last thing you cried about? She went quiet at that one, and then said, "A voicemail. I'm not going to tell you whose."

It was the pause that got me. Pauses are expensive to fake, the old engineers used to say. Then I remembered the newer engineers, who could fake anything, and the pause curdled in my chest into something worse than doubt.

She noticed, because she noticed everything. We were on the lighthouse balcony, and the sea below was doing its scripted, gorgeous glitter.

"You're doing it again," she said.

"Doing what?"

"Looking at me like I'm a math problem." She leaned on the rail. "Let me tell you what it's like on my side. I met a man in a place that's supposed to be mine alone. He knew the lighthouse door was fake. He never walked through the town the way a program would, in a loop. He stopped for no reason to look at a dog. And I thought, *that's either a person or the best-written character I've ever met.* And I haven't been able to tell for three weeks."

I stared at her. "You think *I'm*..."

"I counted your fingers on the first day." She almost smiled. "Twice."

---

We argued about it, then, for what felt like hours. The sea stayed lit and the sun held at the same perfect angle, and neither of us could do a thing about it.

"There's no test," I said finally. "If a sim is good enough to lie, it's good enough to pass anything we can think of."

"So we can't know."

"Not in here."

"Then out there." She said it quickly, as if she'd been holding it for days. "The real one. Pell Street, in the city. There's a laundromat with a blue door. Saturday, seven in the morning. Nobody sane is awake then."

"And if I walk in and you're not there?"

"Then I was a very good product, and you'll have lost nothing but a Saturday."

"And if you are there?"

"Then bring quarters," she said. "The machines don't take cards."

---

Saturday, the city was gray, wet, and unflatteringly real. My knees hurt. I had a crick in my neck from my own bad mattress, and nobody had designed that for me.

The blue door stuck in its frame. Inside, fluorescent light buzzed over a row of dented machines, and a woman sat on a folding chair with a laundry bag between her feet, sneezing into her elbow.

She wore mismatched socks, one with little cartoon sharks. Her hair was flat on one side from the pillow. The fleck in her left eye was exactly where I remembered it.

"You came," Wren said, and then sneezed again. "Sorry. I have a cold. I didn't think they'd put colds in the Bay."

"They don't."

"No." She wiped her nose, looked at me, and laughed, one short astonished sound. "You look terrible."

"You have a shark on your foot."

"It's my lucky sock."

I sat down beside her. We watched the dryers turn. I'd like to say that something clicked, that some final proof arrived: a scar, a phrase, a flicker of the world's seams. Nothing did. The city was too convincing, and so was she. The rain on the window might have been a rendering, and so might the quarter in my palm, whose edges were worn smooth by a thousand thumbs. It could all be one more layer. The Lulls had gotten that good, and so had everything else.

I understood, sitting there, that I would never find a seam. Nobody would. That door had been closed for everyone a long time ago, and we'd all just kept knocking.

"I can't prove you're real," I said.

"I can't prove it either."

"So what do we do?"

She pulled a crumpled tissue from her pocket and considered it. "Same thing as everybody else, I guess. Pick a way to treat each other and see if it holds up."

"That's not a test."

"No," she said. "It's a decision."

The dryer buzzed. Somewhere in a machine or a mind or a wet gray morning that may or may not have been made of light, a warm towel was waiting to be folded. I held out my hand, five fingers, and she took it, and I didn't count hers.

"Quarters?" she asked.

"I brought twelve."

"Good," said Wren. "I have a lot of socks."
