prompt: `` Some men just want to watch the world burn , and darling , you 're the match . ''
content:
# The Match

Desmond Voss kept a fireplace in his office on the fortieth floor, a real one, gas-fed and ridiculous, and he was standing in front of it when Ines Calloway came in with the ledger under her arm.

"You're early," he said, without turning around.

"You said ten."

"I said ten. You came at nine-forty, which means you didn't sleep, which means you've decided." He turned then, smiling the mild smile of a man at a christening. "Sit. Please. I had them bring the good coffee."

She didn't sit. Forty floors below, the city went about its business: the harbor cranes, the courthouse, the glass bank towers, the neat grid of a place that believed in itself. Ines had spent eleven years inside the machinery of that belief. She had balanced its books, and for the last six months she had been quietly learning how many of them were fiction.

"Four hundred million," she said. "Pension funds. Municipal bonds. You moved it through Harlan Shipping and out through the Cayman shells, and you made it look like Marsh and Pell did it. Marsh is dead. Pell is in a hospice. Very tidy."

"Very," Voss agreed.

"You don't even deny it."

"Why would I? You have the proof in your arms. Denial is for people with something to protect." He crossed to his desk and poured two cups, setting one at her place as if she might yet be persuaded to take it. "I'll tell you what you think, Ines. You think I'm a thief. You think this is about the money."

"Isn't it?"

"I have more money than the sum of everyone I've ever met. What would I do with four hundred million more?" He laughed, softly, at the absurdity. "No. The money is kindling. I only needed someone to carry the flame."

She felt the first cold touch of understanding. "You *wanted* someone to find it."

"I wanted *you* to find it." He lifted his cup in a small salute. "Do you know how long I've watched you? You're the only person in that building who reads footnotes. You're careful, you're honest, and you have that terrible, beautiful thing that honest people get, a conscience with no off switch. I left the trail wide enough for a person like that. Not for an auditor. Auditors can be bought, or bored. I needed someone who would *burn* for it."

"Why?"

"Because it's all rotten, darling." He said it tenderly, almost sadly. "The pension boards, the city council, the rating agencies, the newspapers that will run your story and the regulators who will pretend to be shocked. Everyone in this city has been looking away from something for thirty years. It holds together only because no one dares pull the thread. You pull the thread, and the whole sweater comes apart. Banks fail. Bonds crater. Men who were respectable on Monday are in handcuffs by Friday, and the ones who aren't are ruined anyway." His eyes shone. "Some men want to build things. Some want to rule them. And some men just want to watch the world burn. I'm not ashamed to be the third kind. It's the only honest ambition left."

"And I'm what, your instrument?"

"You're the match." He said it gently, the way you would give someone a gift. "Don't take it as an insult. A match is a remarkable thing. A little stick of nothing, and it ends empires. But a match can't choose where it falls. That's the tragedy of it, and the glory. You'll hand that ledger to a reporter, and you'll feel righteous, and you'll be *right*, and it will not matter at all, because the fire will go where fire goes."

The coffee steamed between them. Ines looked at the ledger in her arms, the blue cloth cover, the careful columns of her own handwriting in the margins. Six months of her life.

"You're very sure of me," she said.

"I'm very sure of the type."

"That's your mistake, then." She set the ledger down on his desk, squarely, and squared its corners with her fingertips. Voss's smile flickered, uncertain for the first time. "You've spent all this time studying what a match does. You never thought about the hand."

"The hand?"

"A match doesn't strike itself. It doesn't pick the house, or the hour. Somebody *holds* it." She took out her phone and set it beside the ledger, screen up. A red dot pulsed on it. "You've been talking for eleven minutes. I started recording when I stepped off the elevator."

He laughed, a short, genuine bark. "Oh, Ines. A recording of me confessing to a plan to burn a city? Who will it convict? I've said nothing actionable. I've said I like fire. Men say all sorts of things in front of fireplaces."

"You said you left the trail for me. You said you moved the money through Harlan and framed two men, one of whom is dying. You said it all in your own voice, in your own office." She tilted her head. "You were so busy admiring the metaphor, you described the whole crime. A little vanity, Desmond. It's the only thing a man like you ever leaves unguarded."

The mildness had gone out of his face. What replaced it was something older and more honest, the look of a man who had spent his life as the one holding the flame and was now discovering what it felt like to stand near it.

"The ledger alone would have burned everything," he said slowly. "Everyone. The good with the rotten."

"Yes. That's what you designed it to do. A scandal too big and too tangled to prosecute, so it can only collapse." She picked up her phone. "But a recording isn't a ledger. It has a name in it. One name. It points at one house, and I'm going to carry it there myself, to the one prosecutor in this city I've spent six months making sure was clean. Not a newspaper. Not a bonfire. A *door*, Desmond, with a lock, and a judge on the other side."

"You're a fool. It won't be enough. They'll bury it."

"Maybe." She slipped the phone into her pocket and, after a moment, picked up the ledger again. "But if they do, I'll strike another match. And another. I'll take as many as it takes, one at a time, and I'll choose where every one of them falls. It's slower. It's less beautiful." She walked to the door. "It's called justice. You wouldn't recognize it. It doesn't make nearly so much light."

"Ines." His voice stopped her with her hand on the handle. It was quiet now, almost curious. "Doesn't it frighten you? What you could have done? What you are?"

She looked back at him, small against the enormous window, the city spread out behind him like something he'd been promised.

"Every day," she said. "That's how I know to hold on."

The elevator took forty seconds to reach the lobby. Behind her, in the office on the fortieth floor, the gas fire went on burning in its tidy stone hearth, warming a room that was, for the first time in a long while, entirely and quietly his.

By noon, the first call had gone out. By evening there were men at his door.

And the city, which would never know how near it had come, went on keeping its small, ordinary lights on.

content:
# The Other Chair

The conference was in Columbus, and by the second night I had skipped the networking mixer to drink a bourbon alone at the hotel bar. That was where I found him, three stools down, wearing my face.

He had a better haircut. He'd kept all of it, for one thing, and it was silver at the temples in a way that looked deliberate, like something he'd ordered. His jaw was leaner than mine. He wore a navy jacket that fit him the way clothes only fit people who have never bought anything off a rack.

He saw me see him. He didn't look surprised. He lifted his glass an inch, the way you'd greet a colleague across a conference hall.

"Evan," he said.

"Evan," I said.

"Ev, mostly. Nobody's called me Evan since Rotterdam." He patted the stool beside him. "Come on. You've got the look of a man who needs to be told it's fine."

I should say I didn't doubt it. There are moments when the mind just signs for the package. I took the stool.

---

I'll tell you what I expected. For eleven years, since the summer my father's left hand stopped closing around a coffee cup, I had run a private, well-worn fantasy of the man who got on the plane. The firm in Rotterdam had offered me a position. I was twenty-six, and my drawings had won a prize I still don't like to say out loud. Then Dad had the stroke, and my sister had two toddlers and a husband on the road, and somebody had to be the one who stayed.

I was the one who stayed. I took a job at the county planning office, where I approve septic permits and explain setback requirements to men who are angry about their own property lines. I moved back into my childhood house. I learned to thicken liquids and fill out forms, and how to hear my father's wrecked consonants and translate them for nurses.

In the fantasy, the man who left was a kind of sun, warm and admirable, and I would stand in front of him and feel the full cost of my life in one clean flash. I'd be allowed to grieve properly.

What I felt instead was the same thing I feel when a stranger on a train takes a phone call on speaker.

"What are you drinking?" he asked, and then, without waiting, raised two fingers at the bartender. "Two of the Pappy. The twenty-three, if you've got it." He didn't look at her when he said it. He looked at me, smiling, as if the bartender were a vending machine that had been very good to us.

"I'm fine with what I have," I said.

"Nonsense. It's on me. It's always on me, these days." He laughed, and it was my laugh, but with the corners filed off. "Rotterdam went well, as you'd imagine. Then Singapore. Then a partnership. I did the museum in Lisbon. You'd have liked Lisbon."

"I know the museum," I said. I did. I had once spent a whole lunch break looking at photographs of it on my phone. It was beautiful. Looking at the man who'd made it, I felt something shift, as when you learn that a song you loved was written for a car commercial.

---

He was not a villain. I want to be fair, because I've gone over it many times since.

He was generous in the way of people who've never had to count. He tipped absurdly. He told funny stories, and he told them well, and in every one of them he was the one who saw clearly while everyone around him fumbled. The client who wanted a glass atrium in a hurricane zone. The engineer who cried. The ex-wife, "lovely woman, just wanted a different life than I could give her," delivered with a sigh that was the verbal equivalent of a man checking his reflection in a window.

"And your father?" I asked, finally.

"Ah." He turned his glass a quarter turn on the napkin. "Gone. Nineteen years ago? No. Nine. Pneumonia. It was quick." A pause, perfectly weighted. "I sent flowers. Very good ones. Marcy said they were the biggest at the service."

"You didn't go."

"I was in the middle of a competition bid. You know how it is." He looked at me. "No. You don't, do you."

"Did you call him? Before?"

"Christmas. Birthdays. He wasn't a talker, after." He said *after* the way you'd say the name of a minor town you drove through once. "It was hard to hear him, honestly. It upset me. I felt it was better to remember him as he was."

Something hot and clear rose in me then, and it wasn't envy. I realized I had been braced for envy for eleven years, had built a whole fortress to defend against it, and it turned out the enemy was never going to arrive. What I felt was nearer to recognition. He wasn't some other man. He was a possibility I had carried the whole time, in the same body, the part of me that on bad nights, in the pharmacy line, at the bedside, had wanted so badly to be elsewhere that I could taste it.

He had simply never had to hold it in.

"I don't like you," I said.

I hadn't known I would say it. It came out mild, almost wondering.

He didn't flinch. He studied me for a moment, and for the first time the polish slipped, and I saw underneath it something tired and quick and mean. It was my own expression, the one I make at the office when a man yells at me about a drainage easement.

"That's all right," he said. "I don't much like you either."

"No?"

"You want me to say it? Fine." He leaned in. "You wear it like a medal. Eleven years and I'll bet you have never once let a person forget what you gave up. The sighs. The *well, someone had to.* You didn't stay for him, Ev. Or not only. You stayed because it let you be the good one. You got to be the saint of the situation and also the victim of it, and you never had to find out if you were any good."

The bourbon was very smooth. I drank it anyway and let it burn.

"Maybe," I said.

"Maybe," he agreed, and signaled for the check without looking up, and I understood that this, too, was a kind of answer. He would pay, and tip enormously, and walk out into the rain feeling fine.

---

He stood. He put a hand on my shoulder, and it was warm and heavy and entirely without weight.

"For what it's worth," he said, "the atrium was a good idea. The client was wrong about the hurricane."

Then he was gone through the revolving door, and the glass turned behind him, and I sat looking at the second bourbon he'd bought me. I did not drink it. I left cash for the bartender, more than I could really afford, and looked her in the eye when I thanked her. She seemed startled.

Upstairs, I sat on the hotel bed with my phone. It was nearly eleven. The care home let him keep his own phone, a big-buttoned one my sister had picked out. He'd probably be asleep. I called anyway.

It rang six times. Then there was the soft, clotted breath I know better than my own, and my father's voice, slurred and unhurried and entirely present: "Ehv."

"Hey, Dad. It's me."

"Know it's you." A long pause while the words assembled themselves. "You're. Late."

"I know," I said. "I'm sorry. Tell me what you had for dinner."

He told me. It took four minutes. It was soup.

I listened to every word.

content:
The first thing I noticed was that the kitchen sounded like a different room.

Same toaster, same radio murmuring the weather, same wet slap of Dev's bare feet on the tile. But when Anjali turned from the stove and spoke, the words came out of her as pure music, rolling and tapping, with no little delay in my ear and no soft synthetic voice laying English over the top like a tablecloth.

I smiled and waited for the meaning to arrive.

It didn't.

"Sorry," I said. "Say again?"

She frowned and said it again, slower. It was a pleasant sound, like rain on a tin roof, and it meant absolutely nothing to me.

I touched the pearl in my ear. It was warm, as it always was, and dead. No chime and no little blue pulse. Fifteen years of marriage, and I had never once heard the silence under her voice.

"Anjali," I said. "I think the translator's down."

She tilted her head. Her eyebrows went up at the sound of me, and I understood that to her I was only noise as well. She tapped her own ear, then pointed at me, and her face moved through confusion and dawning alarm.

"Yes," I said, nodding like an idiot. "Yes. Broken. Everything."

Priya came in then, nine years old, hair half-braided, wearing the oversized yellow raincoat she had insisted on wearing indoors since her Japanese phase began. It was the third phase this year. The year before there had been Portuguese, after a cartoon, and before that a long season of Swahili when she'd fallen in love with a documentary about elephants. The translator made it all so easy. A child could pick a language like a flavor of ice cream, speak it at the dinner table, and be understood perfectly by everyone. I had thought it was wonderful. I had told people at work it was wonderful.

"Otōsan," she said brightly, and then something long and quick. I caught *otōsan*, which meant me, because she'd been calling me that for three weeks. The rest slid past.

"Good morning, sweetheart," I said. "The, uh. The ears are broken."

She stared at me. Then her face crumpled in the particular way a child's does when the world has done something it isn't allowed to do. She turned to her mother and began to talk, fast and rising, and Anjali answered in her low steady Tamil, and the two of them went back and forth in languages that were not the same as each other's or mine. I stood between them like a man at a border with no papers.

Dev arrived last, six years old, dragging his blanket. He spoke Tamil, his mother's language, because his grandmother had lived with us the winter he learned to talk, and it had stuck. He said something to Anjali, and she answered, and he looked at me and said something else, small and questioning.

"I don't know, buddy," I said. "I'm sorry. I don't know."

His lip trembled. He held up his cup, empty, and shook it.

*That* I understood.

"Milk," I said, and crossed to the fridge and poured it, and he took the cup and gave me a look of such grave relief that my throat tightened. Milk, at least. The old language, the one before language, where you held up a cup and someone filled it.

We sat down to breakfast like four people at a diplomatic summit.

Anjali had made idli, because it was Saturday, and set out the little bowls of chutney. I reached for the coconut one, and she said a word, sharp and quick, and moved it away. I froze. She pointed at it, then at Dev, then made a face and fanned her mouth.

"Spicy," I said. "Too spicy. For him?"

She nodded, although she couldn't have understood me, and I realized I hadn't needed to. I had understood *her*. I had read it in the lift of her hand, the quick crease between her eyes, the way she angled her body toward our son even as she spoke to me. I had seen this gesture a thousand times without once attending to it, because the pearl had always handed me the meaning first and let the rest of her blur into background.

Priya had been quiet, watching. Now she slid out of her chair, went to the pantry, and came back with the big fraying atlas she loved. She laid it open on the table between the idli and the juice, flipped to Japan, and put her finger on it. Then she pointed at herself. Then she pointed at Anjali, flipped pages, and set her finger on southern India. Then she pointed at me and, after some searching, found England, where my grandparents were from, and tapped it twice.

"Yes," I said. "That's us. All of us."

She nodded gravely. Then she did something I didn't expect. She put one hand on her chest and said slowly, one word at a time, in Japanese, "Watashi wa Priya desu." I had heard her say it before and never noticed it, because it had always arrived in my ear as *I am Priya.* Now it was just sounds, and it was a small brave thing she was handing me.

"Priya," I said, and put my hand on my chest. "Daniel."

She giggled. "Dan-ee-eru."

Dev wasn't going to be left out. He pointed at his bowl and said, "Idli."

"Idli," I said.

He pointed at the chutney and said a word.

"Say it again."

He said it again. I tried it and got it wrong. He corrected me with merciless patience, and I tried again, and this time Anjali laughed, a real laugh, surprised out of her. It was the laugh I fell in love with at a conference in Chennai, back when we'd had to use handheld translators the size of paperbacks, back when we had spoken in halting, ridiculous, shared English and every sentence cost us something. I had forgotten that. I had forgotten that the cost was where the meaning lived.

She said something to me then, quietly, and held my eyes. It was long, and her voice had gone soft. I didn't understand a single word, and I understood that it mattered.

I did the only thing I could. I reached across the table and took her hand. She squeezed it. Her eyes were bright.

"I'm sorry," I said. "I don't know your language. Fifteen years. I never learned it. I always thought I didn't have to."

She shook her head slowly, smiling, and said something that sounded like *it's all right,* and perhaps it was, or perhaps it was *pass the salt.* I would never know. But I understood the squeeze of her fingers, and for the first time in a long time I did not feel I was being translated. I felt I was being *met.*

The pearl chimed in my ear.

"Service restored," the soft voice said. "We apologize for the interruption."

Everything snapped into focus. Anjali's voice slid into English, warm and clear: "—and I said I've missed this, Daniel. I've missed you trying. Do you know, you haven't tried in years."

I looked at her. The kids were chattering at once, Priya about Tokyo, Dev about chutney, a bright waterfall of meaning, and none of it had the weight the silence had.

"Say it again," I said. "In Tamil."

She blinked. "Why?"

"Because I want to hear what it actually sounds like."

She said it again, the same music, and this time I listened to the shape of it and not the meaning. Then I reached up, took the pearl from my ear, and set it beside my plate.

"Teach me," I said. "Starting with *chutney.*"

Dev groaned, delighted, and said the word again, slow and loud, the way you speak to someone very far away who is finally coming closer.

prompt: Your body morphs every night , you alternate every day as a man and a woman . You try to slip out of your one-night stand 's apartment before he wakes up to see the transformation .
content:
# Pins and Needles

The phone was dead, and that was the first mistake.

I knew it before I opened my eyes, because the room was too bright for 3 a.m. and my body had the humming, fizzing feeling of a foot waking up, only it was my whole self. Pins and needles from scalp to heel. The change was already finished, or nearly.

I lay still and took inventory.

Hips: wider. Chest: heavier. Hair: longer, tangled across my neck. When I swallowed, my throat felt smaller. Yesterday I had been Sam, six-foot-one with a beard I never managed to keep even. Today I was Sam with a different set of parts, and I was in a stranger's bed.

Beside me, a man named Theo was asleep on his stomach, one arm flung over his head, snoring in small, polite puffs.

*Okay,* I thought. *Okay. Clothes. Door. Go.*

I had a system for this, and the system was simple: never be asleep at 4 a.m. I'd leave by two or set an alarm for three. I had once spent a whole night in a laundromat to avoid an awkward conversation. But Theo had made me laugh at the bar, then laughed at himself for laughing, and his apartment had smelled like cardamom, and somewhere between his second story and his third I had stopped watching the clock. I'd plugged my phone into his charger. It was the wrong cable. Of course it was.

I slid one leg out from under the sheet, an inch at a time.

The floor was cold. My jeans lay by the closet, and I knew without trying them that they were a lost cause. They'd been cut for a man's hips and a man's legs, and now they'd hang off me like a flag on a windless day. My shirt, a gray button-down, would be fine if I didn't mind looking like I'd robbed someone. My shoes would slide around my feet. My watch would spin on my wrist.

I collected it all in a pile against my chest. Boxers, jeans, shirt, one sock. Where was the other sock?

Behind me the snoring stopped.

I froze, bent over like a burglar, one hand on the bedpost.

The mattress creaked. Theo exhaled, a long sigh, and rolled onto his side. I counted five seconds, then ten. The snoring resumed.

*Sock's not worth it.*

I tiptoed into the hall. His apartment was small and warm, with a bookshelf that had been organized by someone who loved it and then abandoned it. On the fridge there was a photo-booth strip of Theo and an older woman making increasingly ridiculous faces. In the kitchen I stopped to dress in the gray light from the window above the sink.

The boxers stayed up if I knotted the waistband. The jeans I rolled at the ankles and cinched with the belt to the last hole, then one more hole that I made by stabbing the leather with a fork tine. The shirt hung to mid-thigh, which was either a look or a cry for help. I had no bra. That was a problem for outdoors, not for here.

I was reaching for my shoes by the front door when I heard the voice.

"There's coffee, if you want it."

I did not scream. I'm proud of that. I made a sound like a kettle and turned around.

Theo was sitting at the small table by the window, which I had walked past in the dark without noticing. He wore a bathrobe and held a mug in both hands. His hair was flattened on one side. He looked tired and entirely awake, and he did not look horrified, which was the thing I'd been braced for all these years.

"How long," I said. My voice came out higher than I'd expected, and I winced.

"Since about four." He nodded toward the bedroom. "I woke up and you were glowing a little. Not, like, *glowing* glowing. More like when you hold a flashlight under a blanket." He considered. "Then I thought I was dreaming. Then I got up and made coffee and decided I wasn't."

"Right." My heart was going so hard I could feel it in my teeth. "Okay. So. I'll just—"

"Does it hurt?"

I stopped with my hand on the doorknob.

Nobody had ever asked me that. In eleven years, there had been exactly three people who knew, and they'd all asked *how* or *why* or, once, memorably, *can you do it on command?* Never *does it hurt.*

"Not really," I said. "It's like your whole body falls asleep and wakes up. Itchy. Then it's done."

"That sounds awful."

"It's mostly just inconvenient." I looked down at my belted jeans. "As you can see."

He laughed, a short surprised laugh, then pressed his lips together. "Sorry. I'm not laughing at you."

"You can laugh at the fork thing. I did a fork thing."

"I heard the fork thing." He stood and went to the counter. "I wasn't going to say anything. I was going to let you sneak out, because it seemed like you really wanted to, and I figured I'd respect that. But then you were doing the *belt*, and I just—" He gestured helplessly. "I have sweatpants. They have a drawstring."

I should have said no. I should have said thank you, no, and walked out in my terrible jeans, because that was the system, and the system had kept me safe for eleven years.

But the system had also kept me alone in a lot of laundromats.

"Does it happen every night?" he asked, pouring a second mug. "The change?"

"Every night. Sometime between three and five. Man one day, woman the next. Back and forth." I took the mug. It was hot enough to hurt, in a good way. "Yesterday I was a guy. You met a guy."

"I met you," Theo said.

"That's not—"

"I mean, you were the one at the bar. You were the one who said the thing about the pigeons." He sat across from me. "Same person laughing at the same stupid jokes. Seemed like you."

I stared into the coffee. My eyes were doing something embarrassing. "Most people want to know which one's the real one."

"Is there one?"

"No." I laughed, wet and surprised. "Both. Neither. It's just Tuesday."

"It's Wednesday."

"Then it's a Wednesday kind of me."

He smiled, and it was the same smile from the bar, a little crooked, a little shy. Outside, a garbage truck groaned down the street and the sky went from gray to pale gold.

"So," Theo said. "I make okay eggs. And I have sweatpants. And I'd like to hear about the pigeons again, if you're not in a rush."

I thought about the door, and the street, and the long walk home in a stranger's belt.

Then I thought about the strip of photos on the fridge, all those ridiculous faces, and how he had kept the coffee hot for an hour without waking me.

"I'm not in a rush," I said.

He got up to find the sweatpants, and I sat in the warm kitchen with one sock and a cup of coffee. For the first time in eleven years, I let the morning come.

prompt: Description of your favourite meal
content:
# The Pot on the Back Burner

My favourite meal is not impressive. No one has ever photographed it. It arrives in a dented aluminum pot, and it is the color of a warning sign.

It is my mother's kimchi jjigae, and I have been trying to make it for eleven years.

---

The first thing you must understand is the kimchi. My mother kept a jar in the back of the refrigerator that she called "the old one." It had fermented so long it had lost its crunch and gone soft and tangy, sour enough to make your jaw ache. Fresh kimchi is for eating with rice. The old one is for cooking, because heat turns its sharpness into something deep and rounded, almost sweet.

She would start with pork belly, cut thick, and drop it into the dry pot. It hissed and sputtered, and the kitchen filled with the smell of rendering fat. Then came the kimchi, cold and dripping, which hit the pan with a sound like applause. She stirred it with a long-handled spoon worn thin on one side, and a spoonful of gochugaru went in. A little sesame oil followed, and then the garlic. By then the whole apartment smelled like home, and I would drift in from my homework without being called.

Water went in last, and then the waiting. That was the part I hated as a child and love now. The pot sat on the back burner, muttering to itself, while the rice cooker on the counter counted down its own small mystery. My mother would slide in blocks of tofu, pale and trembling, and a handful of sliced scallions. Then she'd stand with her arms crossed, watching the surface bubble, as if the stew might try something.

"Not yet," she'd say, when I lifted the lid. "It's still thinking."

---

When the rice cooker clicked, the ritual sped up. She scooped rice into two bowls, shaping each into a dome as smooth as a river stone. Then she fried an egg in the little pan, in oil hot enough that the white blistered and lace-edged itself into crisp gold. The yolk stayed loose. She slid one egg onto each mound of rice.

The jjigae came to the table still boiling, in the pot itself, set on a folded dish towel. Red broth, bobbing tofu, soft ribbons of kimchi, the pork gone tender and translucent at the edges. Steam rose and fogged my glasses. I would take off my glasses, and my mother would laugh.

The first bite was always too hot. I'd take it anyway: a spoonful of broth over rice, the yolk breaking and slicking everything gold, the heat arriving in two waves, first the sour and then the slow burn behind it. My eyes watered. My nose ran. My mother pushed the napkins toward me without a word, and we ate in the happy silence of two people who didn't need to talk.

She worked double shifts at the dry cleaner's then. This meal was what she made when she came home too tired to make anything else, which is to say it was what she made when she made the most. Only later did I understand that the stew was never really about the pork or the kimchi. It was the one hour of the day when she sat down.

---

I left for college, then for a job in a city where the grocery stores sold only the fresh kimchi, bright and crisp and wrong. I tried anyway. I made the stew in a thin pot, with the wrong pork and too much water, and it tasted like punishment: thin, sharp, and flat. I tried a dozen times. I called her once, frustrated, and she said, "You're not letting it think."

Last winter I flew home. She was sixty-eight and had finally cut back her hours. Her hands, I noticed, had begun to shake a little when she held the spoon.

"Sit," I said. "I'll cook."

She sat at the table and watched me with her arms crossed, the way she once watched the pot. I took out the old jar. I let the pork hiss in the dry pan, and I let the kimchi hit it like applause. I measured nothing. I added the water and then I did the hardest thing I know how to do. I stepped back and waited.

"Not yet," she said, when I reached for the lid.

I fried the eggs. I shaped the rice into domes, badly. I carried the pot to the table on a folded dish towel, and the steam fogged my glasses. I took them off. My mother laughed.

She took the first spoonful, closed her eyes, and was quiet for so long that I thought I had failed again.

"Too much garlic," she said at last, and then she smiled. She reached across the table and pushed the napkins toward me, because my eyes were already watering, and not only from the heat.

We ate in the happy silence of two people who didn't need to talk. And that is my favourite meal: red broth, a broken yolk, and a small kitchen where for one hour no one is in a hurry.

content:
# The Season of Visiting

On the morning I turned eighteen, my father made pancakes shaped like countries.

"This one's Portugal," he said, sliding a lopsided blob onto my plate. "Or Ohio. I've lost the knack."

He was a cartographer, so he had opinions about borders, mostly that they were temporary. Under the Accord, they were also optional for anyone under eighteen. Children belonged to their families, their streets, and their languages, but not to flags. We carried gray Ward cards, which let us go to school, see doctors, and ride trains. Then came the Season of Visiting, twelve months to look, and the Declaration, when you stood in front of a clerk and said *this one.*

My brother Tomas had chosen Aurelia at eighteen. Low taxes, fast trains, a pension system that people described in the reverent voice usually reserved for cathedrals. He sent postcards of glass buildings. *Efficient here,* he wrote. *You'd hate it. Come anyway.*

"Do you want me to tell you what I'd pick?" my father asked.

"No."

"Good. I wouldn't." He smiled. "I chose Karesh when I was your age, and then I spent thirty years learning what I'd actually chosen. It's not the same as the brochure."

"Is anything?"

"Marriage," he said. "Sometimes. Eat your Ohio."

---

The Season began with the Fair.

Every Ward in the region was marched through the Exposition Hall in Geneva-on-the-Lake, where each country had a pavilion and a staff of recruiters who were very good at looking like they weren't recruiting. Aurelia had a fountain that poured light. Nordmark gave out free wool socks. The Karesh Federation had long tables where strangers were fed soup and asked about their grandmothers. The Pacific Concord had a wave machine, which seemed like cheating.

I took pamphlets until my bag cut into my shoulder. They all said the same things in different fonts: *Freedom. Belonging. Opportunity. Home.*

"It's like being courted by forty very tall, very patient suitors," said Odile, my best friend, who had already decided on Nordmark because she liked the idea of snow as a civic institution. "You just have to ask which one lies least."

"They all lie."

"Sure. But how?"

That became my project for the Season. I stopped reading what the countries said about themselves and started looking for how they hid things.

---

In Aurelia, I stayed with Tomas for three weeks. It was beautiful, and no one was ever late. When I asked a woman on the train why the stations had no benches, she said, "Why would you sit? The next train is ninety seconds away." Tomas worked fourteen hours a day and called it *momentum.* One night I found him on the balcony not looking at anything.

"Are you happy?" I asked.

"I'm *productive,*" he said, and then, hearing himself, laughed until he had to wipe his eyes. "Ask me again in a year."

In Karesh, I was fed continuously and consulted constantly. There was a vote on the placement of a bus stop, and I was invited to it as a guest, and I sat through four hours of passionate disagreement over eleven meters of pavement. Everyone was kind. Nobody could be alone without being asked if they were all right. I loved it for nine days and wanted to scream on the tenth.

In Nordmark, the snow was a civic institution, as promised. So was silence. A man at the border office told me proudly that in his country no one ever asked you a question you hadn't invited. I thought of my father's kitchen, where questions came flying from every direction like dishes, and felt homesick for noise.

I visited eleven countries in all. In each I asked the same thing of whoever would answer: *What's the worst thing about living here?*

Most people laughed it off. Some got defensive. A few told me real things, but only when they were sure no official was listening. None of it was in the pamphlets, of course, and none of it was lies, exactly. It was just what you learn once you stop being a guest.

---

By month ten, I was exhausted and no closer to knowing. Odile had signed her preliminary papers. Half my classmates had too. The rest of us moved through the Season like people at the end of a very long party, still smiling, wondering where our coats were.

"You don't have to pick the best," my father said one evening, not looking up from a map he was redrawing. A river had changed its mind again. "You know that. There isn't a best."

"Then what am I picking?"

"Who you're going to be angry at." He tapped the river. "Everyone's angry at their country eventually. Pick the one you'll want to fix."

I thought about that for a long time.

---

The last country I visited wasn't on the Fair's main floor. It was in a corner by the loading dock, a folding table with a hand-lettered sign: *THE REPUBLIC OF SAINT-ELOI.* It was one of the small ones, a river valley, population four hundred thousand, famous for nothing. The woman behind the table was eating a sandwich and didn't stand up when I approached.

"Take a pamphlet," she said. "It's not good."

It was a single folded sheet. On the front, a photograph of a town, slightly overexposed. Inside, under the heading *What We Offer,* was a short paragraph. Under the heading *What We Haven't Fixed,* was a much longer one.

*Our flood barriers fail every eleven years or so. Our two largest parties have not agreed on anything since 1994. The northern district was treated badly for decades and has not forgotten, and neither should you. Our trains are late. Our bureaucracy is slow and sometimes petty. We lose about a third of our young people to Aurelia. If you come, we will need you to stay, and we cannot promise you'll be glad you did.*

At the bottom: *We can promise that you will be useful.*

I read it twice. "Is this allowed?"

"Technically, it's not *prohibited,*" the woman said. "The Ministry of Persuasion keeps sending me notes."

"Does it work?"

"Not at all." She finished the sandwich. "We get maybe nine Declarations a year from the Fair. But the nine who come tend to stay."

I spent my last month in Saint-Eloi. It was not beautiful. The trains were late. A man at the municipal office was rude to me for forty minutes about a form, and then, when he understood I was a Ward and not a complainant, walked me to the right window himself and apologized. The river smelled like a river. I helped sandbag a barrier in a drizzle at midnight with a hundred strangers, and nobody asked me my citizenship, and afterward someone handed me a thermos of something hot and terrible and said, "Well, that's one more year."

I stood there in the dark, soaked and aching, and thought: *Oh. It's this. It's being counted on.*

---

On Declaration Day, the Hall was full of families in good clothes. My father sat in the third row beside Tomas, who had flown in and looked thinner. Odile waved from across the aisle, already half Nordmarkian in a wool scarf.

The clerk was a tired man with a stamp. "State your name and your choice."

"Wren Halloran-Voss," I said. "Saint-Eloi."

He paused. "You're certain?"

"No," I said. "But I'm choosing it anyway."

I thought he might argue, but he only smiled slightly and brought the stamp down. It was heavier than I expected, a real sound, like a door.

"The Accord permits one renunciation," he said, reciting. "Should you ever wish to choose again."

"I know."

"Most people don't use it."

"I know that too."

Outside, my father hugged me for a long time. "Saint-Eloi," he said into my hair. "That's the one with the floods."

"Every eleven years."

"I'll draw you a better map of the river."

"It'll change its mind."

"They always do," he said. "That's why you have to keep going back."

I carried my new blue card out into the bright cold afternoon. It didn't feel like belonging, not yet. It felt like a promise made in a language I'd just begun to learn.

But it was mine. I had chosen it, with my eyes open, and I knew exactly what I'd be angry at.

That seemed like a good place to start.

content:
# The Spider on Orrin's Crown

The webs appeared the autumn after the old bridge collapsed, and by first snow they had swallowed the whole of Harrow Pass.

Tamsin Vael had watched them grow from her father's rope-walk in the village of Under-Orrin. At first they were threads, silver filaments drifting between the crags like hair in water. Then they thickened into cables, then sheets, until the upper mountain looked wrapped in a vast white shroud, and at its center, on the summit, something moved that was larger than a house.

Nine caravans had gone up since the webs began. None had come down.

"Behemoth Peak Spider," said old Corwen, the village elder, tapping his pipe against the council table. "My grandmother called her Ysolka. A story to frighten children. Now the grain won't cross, the salt won't cross, and by midwinter we'll be eating the seed corn."

"Then someone should talk to her," Tamsin said.

The room laughed, but not for long. Tamsin was twenty-two and had climbed Orrin's lower faces since she could walk. She could tie forty knots blind and read ice the way scholars read script. She was also the only person in the village who'd ever bothered to look at the old stories properly.

"Ysolka's tale has a second half," she said. "The one nobody tells. In it, the spider doesn't just eat anyone who climbs. She *answers* anyone who challenges her fairly. Three times in the old stories, someone climbed up and called her out, and three times she accepted."

"And what happened to them?"

Tamsin shrugged. "Two died. The third came back."

---

She climbed alone, because no one else would go and because a challenge, in the stories, was always made by one voice.

She took her father's best rope, two ice axes, a coil of hemp cord, a bell of village bronze, and a clay jar of lamp oil. The webs began at the second shelf. Up close they were not white but faintly translucent, humming in the wind like a plucked string. Each strand was as thick as her wrist. She touched one with her glove, and it stuck fast, and somewhere far above, something felt it.

The mountain went still. Then a voice came down the slope, dry and slow, like rock sliding over rock.

"*Small one. You climb loudly.*"

Tamsin's heart hammered. She had expected screeching, or nothing. She had not expected to be spoken to like a guest who'd tracked in mud.

"I climb honestly," she called. "I've come to challenge you, Ysolka."

A long silence. Then the web trembled, and a leg emerged from the cloud above, black and jointed and tall as a pine, tipped with a claw the color of old ivory. It tested the ledge twenty paces from her. After it came the rest.

Ysolka was not what the stories had said. She was bigger, and she was old. Her body was the size of a barn, gray-furred and scarred, with a cluster of eyes like dark lanterns. One leg was missing at the second joint, healed over with knots of silk. She settled onto the crag above Tamsin, and the whole mountain seemed to lean.

"*No one has used that word in a long time,*" the spider said. "*Challenge. Say what you mean by it.*"

Tamsin's mouth was dry. She'd rehearsed this part for three nights. "A contest. If I win, you open the pass. If you win..." She swallowed. "You keep me, like the others."

"*The others were not challengers. They were passengers. They flew into my web and I ate them. I am a spider.*" The eyes glittered. "*But a challenge is another matter. Name the contest.*"

"A weaving," said Tamsin.

The spider made a sound that might have been laughter. "*You propose to out-weave me.*"

"I propose to cross the gap at the Needle's Eye before you do." She pointed to where two spires leaned together, a hundred and fifty feet of empty air between them, wind screaming through the notch. "You spin your bridge. I make mine. First to anchor on the far side wins."

"*I could cross that in a breath.*"

"Then you'll win quickly," Tamsin said, "and I'll have lost nothing I wasn't already going to lose."

Ysolka regarded her for a long moment. Then she turned her great head toward the Needle's Eye, and Tamsin realized, with a lurch, that the spider was *interested*.

"*Done,*" said Ysolka.

---

They stood on the western spire, the wind yanking at Tamsin's coat. Ysolka crouched beside her, vast and patient.

"*Begin when you wish,*" the spider said.

Tamsin did not begin by building. She uncoiled her hemp cord, tied it to the bronze bell, and flung the bell across the gap. It clanged against the far rock and caught in a crack. She had practiced that throw for years, hurling stones across the river back home. Then she looped the line through a pulley of her own making and began hauling her heavy rope over, strand by strand.

Ysolka was already spinning. A silver thread shot across the gap, glittering, and fastened on the far spire in a single heartbeat. Then another. Then a dozen. The bridge assembled itself in the air, impossibly fast, strand over strand.

It should have been over. But the wind at the Needle's Eye was a living thing, and it howled through the notch and plucked at the new silk. The strands sang and swayed, and where they swayed they tangled with one another, and the bridge began to knot itself into a snarl.

"*Ah,*" said Ysolka quietly. She began to repair, and every repair took time, because the wind undid what it could.

Tamsin's rope bridge went slowly. It was ugly, heavy, tied in dull hemp. But she had spent her life making ropes that held in wind. She spliced a weighted line beneath it, tied cross-braces to damp the sway, and let the bridge hang slack and low where the gusts passed over. It did not sing. It simply hung.

By the time Ysolka's silver span was half-mended, Tamsin was on her own rope, crawling across, wind clawing at her, boots scraping the cords. She gained the far side, drove an axe into the stone, and knotted off the final anchor.

"Done," she gasped.

On the opposite spire the great spider stood motionless, her silver bridge swinging in tatters behind her.

"*Done,*" Ysolka agreed.

---

Tamsin expected to die then. She stood on the far spire, trembling, as the spider crossed the hemp bridge with surprising delicacy, testing each strand with her claws, and settled in front of her. The eyes caught the light.

"*You didn't fight the wind,*" Ysolka said. "*You gave it nothing to hold.*"

"My father taught me. A rope that argues with the wind loses."

"*Your father is wise.*" The spider was silent for a time. "*I have spun on this mountain for four hundred winters. Do you know why the webs have grown so thick this year?*"

"I thought you were hungry."

"*I am old and slow, and the mountain is breaking.*" One leg gestured, and Tamsin followed it. Beyond the pass, high on the north face, a long dark fissure ran through the glacier, a crack she had never seen from below. "*The ice is sliding. The bridge you lost fell because the slope under it moved. My webs hold the ice. Every strand is an anchor. If I stop spinning, the glacier comes down, and your village sleeps under it.*"

Tamsin stared. The "shroud" she had feared was a net holding the mountain together.

"And the caravans?"

"*Walked into the anchors. I did not ask them to. I do not leave my work, and I must eat.*" A pause. "*I am not proud of it.*"

Tamsin thought about the nine caravans, the families waiting, the grain. She thought about the village under the glacier. She thought, strangely, about her father's hands.

"A bargain, then," she said. "Not a surrender. You hold the ice. We keep the pass clear, a corridor, marked with bells so travelers know where the webs are. Villagers climb up twice a season with rope and hemp to reinforce your anchors, so you spin less and tire less. And in exchange..."

"*In exchange?*"

"We bring you food. Goats, sheep. Enough that you never need to take a traveler again."

The spider's eyes shifted in the pale light. When she spoke again, her voice had changed, softer, like a stone worn smooth.

"*No one has bargained with me in three hundred years,*" said Ysolka. "*Only fled, or prayed, or died.*" The scarred head dipped. "*You challenged fairly, small one. You won fairly. I accept your terms.*"

---

Tamsin came down the mountain two days later. Behind her, a path of bronze bells trembled along the pass, marking a safe way through the silver. At the bottom, the villagers were waiting. Corwen stood at the front, pipe forgotten in his hand.

"Well?" he said. "What did she say?"

Tamsin looked back up at the peak, where in the last light something enormous and gray lifted a single leg in what might have been a wave.

"She said the mountain's been holding us up all this time," Tamsin said, "and it was about time someone held back."

That spring the first caravan crossed Harrow Pass in safety, bells chiming in the thin air. And every season afterward, the people of Under-Orrin climbed to the Needle's Eye with rope and goats and lamp oil, to visit the old spider who kept the sky from falling.

content:
# The Last Names

The rule is older than any of us, and nobody remembers who wrote it. A hero does not die of age, or a blade, or a bullet. A hero dies only by choosing someone else, putting a hand on a stranger's shoulder and saying *you*. Then the weight moves, the old body finally rests, and a new one stands up and begins.

I have never done it. I am four thousand and some years old, depending on whose calendar you trust, and I have never once said *you*.

I had been thinking about it for sixty years.

---

The plan was a bus station. I would stand in the middle of the morning crowd, close my eyes, turn in a slow circle, and put my hand out. Whoever I touched would get the strength, the long life, and the thing in the chest that wakes you before the screaming starts. Random was the only honest way I could think of. Every hero who chose carefully chose wrong. They picked the brave, and the brave burned out in a decade. They picked the kind, and the kind went bitter. The ones who picked their own children, God help them, buried their children's patience long before they buried the children.

So: a bus station, a hand, and then rest.

I had already bought the ticket. I was sitting at my kitchen table with it propped against the sugar bowl when the letter came through the slot.

It wasn't in an envelope. It was a single sheet folded in thirds, stiff and brown at the creases. I knew what the brown was before I unfolded it, because I have smelled that smell on every battlefield since bronze.

Five words, in a hand I knew, though the strokes were wet and shaky:

**WE ARE THE ONLY ONES LEFT**

No name. There didn't need to be. Only one person ever crossed his sevens that way, and I had taught him to do it in a tent outside Nineveh.

---

You have to understand what the sentence meant.

There had never been a number. Heroes came and went, and when one chose, another rose. The count rose and fell like a tide, but it never went below a few hundred, because there was always someone to catch the weight. We didn't talk about it much. It was like asking how many stars there were.

*We are the only ones left.*

Two. Him and me. Nobody else.

That should have been impossible. Even if every hero on earth had chosen a successor and died, the successors would still be there, standing in their place. The line couldn't thin. It could only pass along.

Unless someone was taking the successors, too.

I read the letter again and noticed what I'd missed. The blood wasn't dripped or smeared. It had been *written*, by someone with enough time and enough pain to take care over it. He had used his own blood because he had nothing else, and he had taken care because he knew I would need to read every word.

At the bottom, in the corner, in a different pressure of the finger, there was a smudge that was almost a letter. An *S*, or the start of one. Then it trailed off.

*S.* Not his name. A place, maybe, or a word he hadn't finished.

I turned the ticket over. Then I put it in the stove.

---

His name is Ilvane. At least, it is now. He has had others.

We met when the first cities were still mud, and we have been friends in the way only the very old can be, which means we have spent more time apart than most nations last. I once went three hundred years without speaking to him and it felt like a long weekend. When he called, I came. When I called, he came, grumbling.

He was the one who talked me out of choosing the first time I tried, two thousand years ago, when I stood on a cliff with a shepherd boy and couldn't say the word. "Not yet," he'd said. "You'll know when."

I had assumed that was wisdom. Now I wondered if he had known something even then.

The letter had no return address, but heroes can find each other. There's a thread between us, thin as spider silk, and I had always felt it the way you feel a tooth with your tongue. It had been fraying for a long time. I had never counted the strands that were missing. I had never wanted to.

I closed my eyes at the kitchen table and followed it. For the first time in millennia I found only two ends, mine and his. Everything between them was empty.

His end was a long way north. And it was bleeding.

---

It took me four days. I could have been faster, but I made myself slow down and think the way I used to when thinking was most of what the job was.

If someone was killing heroes, they would have to find a way around the rule. We could not be killed. We could only choose. So the question was how you make a hero choose.

You hurt them until they say *you*.

But a hero will name a stranger, a passing child, anyone, before he'll name the man holding the knife. That's how a sane hero thinks.

Unless it didn't matter whom the heroes named. Unless the killer simply made them choose again and again, and followed each new successor to the next, and the next, collecting them like fruit. Each hero broken and spent, each successor found and broken in turn, and the power of every one of them gathered up in a single pair of hands.

How long would that take? Years, if you were patient. Centuries, if you were patient and patient and patient.

Nobody would notice. There was never a count.

---

The house was at the end of a salt road, a gray thing with the windows boarded over. I knew it for a trap the moment I saw it. I walked up to the door anyway.

Ilvane was in the front room, in a chair, and I almost didn't recognize him. He had always been big, a barrel of a man. Now he was a shape under a blanket, and his hands were wrapped in cloth that had been white once.

"You came," he whispered.

prompt: Tell me the story of how the first king became the first king
content:
# The Ferryman's Rope

Before there were kings, there were only people, and people are good at many things but poor at agreeing.

In the valley of the two rivers, where the brown water met the green, there lived two peoples: the Hesh on the north bank and the Marrow on the south. They traded, married, and quarreled in the usual proportions. When they disagreed, they shouted until one side was tired or until someone bled. After that there was a funeral, and after the funeral a grudge, and the grudges piled up like drift against a bridge.

Between the banks lived a ferryman named Teodan.

He was not wise, whatever the songs say. He was a broad, tired man with a bad knee who poled a flat boat across the water for a handful of barley or a fish or a favor. His mother had been Hesh and his father Marrow, and neither family had wanted him, so he built a hut on a spit of mud halfway between and made a living out of belonging nowhere.

That detail matters more than any other in the story.

---

The winter that changed everything came early. The river froze at the edges and the fish went deep. Both peoples had stored grain in the autumn, but the Hesh had lost half of theirs to damp, and the Marrow had lost half of theirs to rats. A woman named Ilsa, who kept count of things with knotted cords, proposed that the two peoples pool what they had in one granary on the high ground, and ration it until spring.

It was a good idea, and it was nearly a miracle that anyone agreed to it. They built the granary together, and Ilsa tied her cords, and for a while the plan held.

Then, in the deep of winter, the cords did not match the sacks.

Eleven measures were missing. It wasn't enough to doom anyone, but it was enough to doom the peace. The Hesh said the Marrow had taken it. The Marrow said the Hesh had done it and were hiding it. Knives came out. Ilsa stood between them holding her cords and shouting numbers that no one wanted to hear.

"We need someone to decide," she said at last.

"Decide what?" said a Hesh elder. "Who is lying?"

"Yes."

"Who would we trust to do it?" said a Marrow elder. "Anyone from your side would favor you, and anyone from ours would favor us."

There was a long, ugly silence, and in it someone said, almost as a joke, "The ferryman."

No one laughed.

---

They crossed the ice to his hut, one delegation from each bank, and told him what they wanted. Teodan listened with his bad knee propped on a stool. When they finished, he said, "No."

"Why not?"

"Because whoever I decide against will hate me, and I live alone on a mud bank." He rubbed his knee. "I'd be a fool to say yes."

"You're the only one who can," said Ilsa.

"That's the problem, not the argument."

But he went, because the alternative was blood, and he had spent his life carrying people over water so they wouldn't have to wade through worse things.

He did not do anything clever. He asked to see the granary, and he asked Ilsa to explain her cords. He walked the floor and found where the damp had crept in and where the rats had chewed through a wall. Then he found a small gap behind the last row of sacks, and in it a nest of straw, a child's blanket, and the husks of stolen grain.

The thief was a boy of nine from the Marrow, whose family had been hungry longer than they'd admitted. His mother had said nothing, because she hadn't known. She wept when she learned of it, and the Hesh, who had been ready to hang someone, found it hard to hang her son.

Teodan thought for a long time, and then he said what he would say, and it satisfied no one fully, which is how you know it was fair. The Marrow would repay the eleven measures from their own share, in spring. The Hesh would not strike the boy. The boy would sweep the granary and help Ilsa count until the thaw. And because the Marrow were hungry, the Hesh would lend them grain against the debt, without interest, in front of witnesses.

Everyone grumbled, and everyone obeyed.

---

After that, people began to cross to his hut.

They came with a disputed boundary, a broken bargain, a bride-price that had gone sour. They came because he had no side, and because he listened until they had run out of words. They paid him in barley, fish, and a better pole for the ferry. Ilsa came too, and without anyone naming it, she began to keep his judgments on cords beside the grain, so that what had been decided could not be argued again.

Soon his hut was too small, and people built him a larger one on the high ground between the banks, in the place where the granary stood. He did not want to move, but a man cannot hear thirty people in a hut built for one. He took a stool with him, the one he had propped his knee on, and sat on it to hear cases. When it broke, someone built him a better one.

That was the first throne. It was a stool, mended.

---

But the part that made him a king, rather than a patient neighbor, came in the spring.

Raiders came down from the hill country, hungry men with copper blades who had also survived the winter by deciding someone else should starve. Scouts brought word of them a day's march away. The two peoples gathered on the high ground, frightened, and they began to argue again, because there was no time to do anything else. Who would fight? Who would guard the children? Who would go to meet the raiders at the narrow ford, where a few could hold against many, and who would stay behind?

Everyone knew that the ones who went to the ford would not all come back.

No assembly could settle it. Every voice was an interested one. The Hesh wanted the Marrow at the ford, and the Marrow the Hesh, and every household wanted its own sons kept safe.

At last Ilsa said, quietly, "Teodan has to choose."

He looked at her as if she had struck him. "I can't choose that."

"Someone must, and you're the only one they'll let."

"You're asking me to send people to die."

"Yes," she said. "I am."

He stood for a while with his hand on the back of his mended stool. Then he named them, thirty-one men and women, from both banks in equal measure, chosen for their aim and their steadiness and, when he could not find a reason, by a plain and terrible guess. He told them where to stand and when to hold. He told the rest to take the children to the high caves.

They held the ford. Nineteen came back.

---

On the evening after the fight, a woman came to his house. Her husband had been one of the twelve. She did not weep or shout. She stood in the doorway and asked a question no one had ever had cause to ask before.

"Who sent him?"

The room went still. A hundred answers were available: *the raiders, the winter, the gods, the need.* All of them were true, and all of them were ways of saying *no one.*

Teodan could have used any of them. Instead he said, "I did."

She looked at him for a long moment. Something in her face eased, though not into forgiveness. It was the look of a person who has finally found the place to set down a weight that had nowhere to rest.

"Then you're the one I'll hold to it," she said.

"Yes."

"Good." She nodded once and left.

---

That is the whole of it, though the songs say more. They say a crown fell from the sky, or a sword was drawn from a stone, or a god laid hands on his head. Those are stories told by later kings, who wanted a grander origin than the truth.

The truth is that when the Hesh and the Marrow gathered at midsummer to give Teodan a name for what he had become, no word existed. They argued about it, which was only natural. In the end Ilsa took the old ferry rope from his boat, frayed and tarred and stiff with years of river, and wove it into a ring. She set it on his head, not as an honor but as a marker, so that in any crowd, in any hour of fear or grief, people would know where to look.

"This is so we can find you," she told him.

"To ask things of me?"

"To blame you," she said. "And to thank you. Both. For the same acts."

He understood then what he had been given, and it was not power. Power came later, to the kings after him, who learned to love the ring and forget the rope. What Teodan was given was the weight that everyone else had set down: the choosing, the naming, the *I did.*

He wore the ring until he died, which was many years later, in a bed, which was rare for kings after him.

They say he never once called himself by the new word. But when the children asked, in the evenings, what he was, he would say, "I'm the one who carries people across."

And that is how the first king became the first king: not by taking up a crown, but by being the one person both shores could trust to bear what neither could carry alone.

content:
# The Weight of Margit

"You want to know why I don't use a gun," Ilse said, and set the cloth bundle on the table between us. "Everyone asks. Guns are loud, and they're a conversation with the whole street. A gun is a shout. I prefer a whisper."

She unrolled the cloth slowly. She never hurried when she touched it.

"Her name is Margit."

"You named your knife?"

"I named my *teacher*. The knife was hers first." Ilse smiled without showing her teeth. "Look, but don't touch. Not yet."

It was smaller than I'd imagined, no longer than my hand from wrist to fingertip, and so narrow it seemed less like a blade than the idea of one. The steel was dark, almost the gray of a storm cloud, with a faint blue shimmer where the lamplight slid along it. There was no shine, no cruel mirror gleam like in films. Margit had been blackened with a mixture of oils and ash, so that she drank the light instead of throwing it back.

"Three-sided," Ilse said. "Like a bayonet, but finer. No edge to speak of. People imagine a knife as something that cuts, but cutting is vulgar, a lot of effort and a lot of mess. Margit doesn't cut. She *parts*. She asks the body to step aside, and the body, which is a very polite thing, does."

I swallowed. She noticed.

"The handle is bone. Whale, very old, from before anyone cared about such things. It's yellowed like a piano key, and the grain has worn smooth where four generations of hands have held it. Here." She turned the knife, and I saw a shallow groove near the guard. "That's where Margit's thumb sat. Mine sits in the same place now. When I first held her, my thumb fit the dent as if it had been waiting for me. I didn't sleep that night."

"Why not?"

"Because I understood that I was part of a line. That the hand before mine was gone, and the hand after mine wasn't born yet, and the only constant was this." She tapped the table beside the blade, not touching it. "A sliver of steel that doesn't care who carries it."

The room was quiet. Rain ticked at the window.

"Balance," she went on. "That's the soul of it. Most people think weight is in the blade or the handle. No. The weight lives in a single point, about a finger's width ahead of the guard. If you rest her on your fingertip right there, she hangs level, perfectly still, like a held breath. Hold her anywhere else and she wants to tip, to fall, to *do* something. But there, she's patient. I've spent whole evenings just balancing her on one finger and watching a candle burn down. Margit taught me that. You cannot be hasty with something this honest."

She rewrapped one corner of the cloth, almost tenderly, as one might tuck a blanket around a sleeper.

"The sound is what I love most, and what I hope you never hear. Drawn from the sheath, she makes no sound at all. I had the leather lined with felt and rubbed with beeswax. The silence is part of the design. Everything about her is designed to take away what the world expects. No flash, no ring of metal, no clatter. People hear a door, a footstep, a glass set down. They never hear Margit."

"And the... the moment?" I asked. My voice came out smaller than I intended.

Ilse looked at me for a long time. The humor left her face, and what replaced it was not cruelty but something worse: tiredness, and honesty.

"The moment is very short," she said. "It's shorter than people think, and it's quieter, and it's much more *intimate* than you want it to be. That's the part nobody tells you. A gun lets you stay far away from it, but a blade teaches you the truth. You're close enough to feel a person's warmth. Close enough to hear the last small change in their breathing. Margit doesn't let me pretend, and that's why I keep her. The day I can do this work and feel nothing, I'll set her down and never lift her again."

She held up a hand before I could speak.

"I've kept her thirty-one years. I've oiled her every Sunday. I've sharpened her on a stone older than both of us, using water, never spit, never oil on the stone, because Margit said oil makes you lazy. I know every scratch. There's a hairline nick near the tip from a night in Antwerp that I'd rather not discuss. I know her the way you know a limp in someone you love."

She slid the bundle across the table toward me, and my stomach turned over.

"Pick her up."

"Ilse, I—"

"Pick her up. Find the groove."

My hand shook as I closed it around the handle. The bone was warm from the lamp, and heavier than I expected, and then, strangely, not heavy at all. My thumb found the dent. It fit, and that frightened me more than anything she had said.

"There," Ilse said softly. "Now you know the first thing. She'll feel like she belongs to you." She leaned back, and her eyes were wet in the lamplight. "That's how she gets everyone."

content:
**Right Now**

Okay. Right now. Right now the fridge is humming and it's a B-flat, or maybe not, I never learned, Dad always said B-flat about everything, the fridge, the car engine, the doorbell, like the whole world was tuned to one note and only he could hear it. Don't stop. Dr. Amara said don't stop. So I won't. My thumb hurts. Why does my thumb hurt? I think I slept on it. I haven't slept, so no. I think I've been pressing it into the edge of the desk this whole time, a little crescent moon dent, there, look at that, a tiny moon on my thumb.

The cursor is blinking like it's impatient. Blink. Blink. I used to think cursors were tiny lighthouses. I used to think a lot of things. I thought if I held my breath past the cemetery on Fulton Street, nobody I loved would die. I held it every single time. I got very good at it. I could do the whole stretch, forty seconds, fifty, my lungs like two fists, and then Grandma died anyway, in March, and I was holding my breath in my head the whole drive to the hospital, which is not the same, which is cheating, which is probably why.

Stop. Don't stop. Keep going.

There's a lemon on the counter. I can see it from here. I bought it nine days ago for a recipe I never made, and now it's slightly wrinkled at one end like it's frowning at me. I should either use it or let it go. Lemon tea. Lemon chicken. Lemon, lemon, lemon, the word starts to sound fake if you say it enough. Lemon. Lemon. Dad planted a lemon tree in the backyard in a climate where lemon trees do not belong, and it gave exactly four lemons in eleven years, and he named them. He named them. Gerald, Susan, and I forget the other two, which is horrible, because he'd have remembered. He remembered everything except the thing that mattered, which was to call me back.

There it is.

Okay. There it is. My hands just went cold, which is funny, because writing is the only thing they're doing, and they've gone cold like they know.

He left a voicemail. Thirty-one seconds. I haven't played it. It's been four months and six days and it sits in my phone between a dentist reminder and a coupon for a mattress store, and I know exactly how long it is because the screen tells me, 0:31, such a small number, like a recipe step, like *simmer for 0:31.* I've held it in my hand a hundred times. I've held my breath over it. Over a voicemail. Over thirty-one seconds.

What if it's only him asking about the car? What if it's the weather? What if it's nothing, and the nothing is the last thing, and I've been guarding nothing like it's a vault? And what if it's something? What if he says my name the way he did, the long way, *Ma-ri-sol,* three beats, a little waltz?

My thumb is bleeding. Not really. It's pink. The moon is pink.

The fridge is still humming. B-flat. I'm going to look it up after this, I'll find out if it's really B-flat, and if it is I'll lose it completely, and if it isn't I'll decide it is anyway.

Outside a bird has started up, which is insane, it's barely four-thirty, the sky is the color of dishwater, and this one stupid bird is just announcing himself to nobody. Good for him. Sing. Sing at the dishwater. I should get up. I should get my phone. It's charging in the other room where I put it so I wouldn't be tempted, like a person hiding cookies from herself.

I don't want to stop typing because when I stop typing I'll have to stand up.

Standing up. Walking down the hall. Eleven steps, I counted once. The hallway floor creaks on step seven, so I'll step over it, or maybe I'll step on it on purpose, let the house make its noise, let something in here talk back.

Lemon. Gerald. Susan. Thirty-one seconds. Breathe out, Marisol. You've been holding it a long time. Past the cemetery. Past the whole long road.

All right. All right, I'm standing. The chair scraped, loud as anything. The bird hasn't stopped. The fridge is still on its one note.

I'm going to go and press play, and I'm going to let it be whatever it is.

Eleven steps.

I'm breathing.

# Timeline of Events

*Prepared by Marianne Doyle at the request of Officer T. Reyes, Fairmont Police Department. Re: Walter J. Doyle, age 79, missing from residence, Tuesday, October 8.*

---

**5:40 a.m.**
I wake to the sound of the front door. Not slamming, just the soft double click of the deadbolt and the knob. I have been listening for that sound for eleven months. I lie there for a few seconds anyway, hoping I dreamed it.

*(Officer Reyes, you said to include everything, even the parts that seem like excuses.)*

**5:42 a.m.**
Dad's bed is empty. His slippers are by the door. His work boots are gone, the ones I keep in the hall closet behind the vacuum because I thought if he couldn't see them he'd forget about them. His jacket is gone too, the gray one with *Fairmont Transit – 31 Years* stitched on the pocket.

**5:50 a.m.**
I search the yard, the garage, and the street in both directions. It is 41 degrees. I am wearing a nightgown and his rain slicker. I call his name in the voice I've learned not to use, the high, frightened one. He hates it. He says, "Marnie, I'm not a dog."

**5:58 a.m.**
I call 911. The dispatcher asks for a description. I say: six feet, white hair, a little stooped, gray jacket. She asks if he has any medical conditions, and I say *Alzheimer's* out loud for maybe the fourth time in my life. It still sounds like I am talking about someone else's father.

**6:10 a.m.**
You arrive, Officer Reyes. You are kind, and you ask where he might go. I say I don't know. He doesn't *go* anywhere anymore. He goes from the recliner to the kitchen table to the bathroom and back.

I realize while I'm saying it that this is not true. He goes somewhere every night, in his head. I just never ask where.

**6:25 a.m.**
You ask me to write a timeline while the other officers search. You say it helps to have something to do with your hands. You're right. I'm writing this at the kitchen table, on the back of a pharmacy receipt, and then I'll copy it neatly because I can't stand the thought of handing you something messy.

**6:40 a.m.**
Things I'm not sure how to time, but which seem important:

- Last night at 8:15 he asked me whether the 14 had come yet. I said, "Not yet, Dad," because the doctor's pamphlet says not to argue. He nodded and said, "She's always late when it rains."
- Three weeks ago he asked me to iron his uniform shirt. I told him it was in storage. He seemed satisfied.
- In July he got lost in the hardware store, a place he's been a thousand times. When I found him he was standing in the plumbing aisle with his hands up, as if holding a steering wheel.

I don't know why I didn't put these together before. Or I do know, and it's that I didn't want to.

**6:55 a.m.**
I tell you about the 14. Route 14 ran from Cutler Street to the Eastside Depot, 5:52 a.m. departure, every weekday for nineteen of his thirty-one years. He used to say the first run of the day belonged to the people nobody thought about: nurses coming off shifts, bakers, a man who cleaned offices and always carried a thermos of tea he'd share with whoever sat behind him.

You write something down. You ask where the route started.

**7:05 a.m.**
Cutler Street is four blocks from here. You send a car. They find nothing, only an empty bench and a shelter with a cracked panel.

**7:20 a.m.**
I remember the route doesn't start at Cutler Street. It *used* to, before the city restructured the lines in 2009. After that the 14 started at the depot, because they cut the first stretch. Dad grumbled about it for a year. He said they'd amputated his bus.

**7:24 a.m.**
I say, "The depot," and you are already on the radio.

---

*(I'm writing the next part later, at home, after. I'm leaving the times as they were because that's what you asked for.)*

---

**7:51 a.m.**
We arrive at the Eastside Depot. The gate is chained, but there's a gap in the fence behind the maintenance building where the chain-link has been peeled back. It has probably been that way for years. Kids use it. Apparently so does my father.

**7:55 a.m.**
Behind the building is the bus graveyard, six or seven retired coaches nosed up against a row of dead sumac. Most have no windows. Most have been stripped of their seats.

One has its door folded open.

**7:58 a.m.**
He is in the driver's seat.

He's sitting very straight, in a way I haven't seen in years. His hands are on the wheel at ten and two. The wheel is the only thing on that bus still intact. His boots are planted, and the gray jacket is zipped to his chin.

He doesn't turn when I say his name. I say it again, softly, the way I should have been saying it all along.

**8:01 a.m.**
He says, without looking at me, "You're late."

I don't know whether he means me or the bus or someone else. I say, "I know. I'm sorry. It was raining."

He says, "She's always late when it rains," and I can't breathe for a second.

**8:03 a.m.**
I climb on. The floor is soft with rot and the whole bus smells like wet leaves and old rubber. I sit down in the first seat behind him, the one the man with the tea used to take. I don't know why I do it. It just seems like the right place to sit.

Officer Reyes, you stay outside. I'll always be grateful. You must have been cold, and you stood there for twenty minutes with your hat in your hand.

**8:05 a.m.**
Dad says, "Full load today."

I say, "Looks like it."

He says, "Nurses mostly." He nods at the empty seats and the empty windows, at the dead sumac pressing in like a crowd. "You've got to take the corners easy, they've been on their feet all night."

I say, "You always did."

**8:09 a.m.**
He asks if I want to hear the stops. I say yes.

He recites them: Cutler, Pruett, Alder Heights, St. Brendan's, Wexler Park, the Mill Road underpass, and on to the depot. Twenty-three stops in all, without a single hesitation. He can't remember my birthday or the name of the dog we had for fourteen years, but he has every stop on Route 14, in order, in a voice I haven't heard since I was nine and rode with him on Take Your Daughter to Work Day.

I ride the whole route with him, and neither of us moves.

**8:31 a.m.**
He says, "Last stop. Everybody off."

He sits for a moment. Then he turns and looks at me, really looks, and his face does something complicated. He says, "Marnie. What are you doing on my bus?"

I say, "Just riding, Dad."

He says, "Well. Next time bring a coat."

**8:35 a.m.**
He lets me take his arm. We walk out past the other dead buses. At the fence gap he stops, puts his palm flat against the side of the last coach, and pats it twice, the way you'd pat a horse.

---

**What the form doesn't have a box for:**

He was missing for two hours and fifty-five minutes. He was not hurt, not lost, and not afraid. By any measure that matters to the department, this case is closed.

But I would like it noted, Officer Reyes, that my father did not wander off. He went to work. He got up in the dark, laced his boots, and walked four miles in the cold to a job he retired from nineteen years ago, because people were waiting and somebody had to get them where they were going.

I've been treating his mind like something leaking away. I think it may be closer to a route. It has lost some of its stops, and the detours get longer, but it still runs, and it still knows where it's headed.

On Thursday I'm going to ask the transit authority whether they'd let an old driver sit in a parked bus for an hour now and then, with his daughter in the seat behind him. If they say no, I'll find another way.

In the meantime I've moved his boots from the back of the closet. They're by the door now, next to his slippers, where he can see them.

**Respectfully submitted,**
**Marianne Doyle**

*P.S. Thank you for standing outside.*
